Let us address, with careful deliberation, this question of pH, for we are presented with a solution formed by the admixture of three distinct substances: 500 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid (CH3COOH), 400 mL of 0.2 M hydrochloric acid, and 300 mL of 0.3 M barium hydroxide; the enquirer asks for the pH of the resultant mixture, and offers the choices A) 1.38, B) 12.62, C) 8.68, D) 8.92.

First, it is prudent to convert the volumes into litres for facility of calculation, and indeed one observes that the total volume amounts to 500 + 400 + 300 = 1200 mL, which is equivalent to 1.2 L; yet one admits with temperate caution that the total volume need not occupy our immediate attention at the outset of the stoichiometric considerations.

We may note, to begin the chemical characterisation, that CH3COOH is a weak acid, that HCl is a strong acid, and that Ba(OH)2 is a strong base; hence it is most curious, and indeed of principal consequence, that the neutralisation reactions between the strong species be examined first, for they proceed to completion and will determine whether the weak acid exerts any remaining influence upon the ultimate pH.

Therefore, I shall compute the moles of hydrogen ions furnished by the HCl and the moles of hydroxide ions furnished by the Ba(OH)2, and thence ascertain which is in excess.

Commencing with hydrochloric acid: 400 mL corresponds to 0.4 L, and at 0.2 mol L^-1 this yields moles of HCl equal to 0.4 L × 0.2 mol L^-1 = 0.08 moles; being a strong acid, HCl dissociates completely, and therefore the moles of H+ present are 0.08.

Next, turning to barium hydroxide: 300 mL is 0.3 L, and at 0.3 mol L^-1 the moles of Ba(OH)2 are 0.3 L × 0.3 mol L^-1 = 0.09 moles; since each formula unit of Ba(OH)2 liberates two hydroxide ions, one obtains moles of OH- equal to 0.09 × 2 = 0.18 moles.

Thus, one has 0.08 moles of H+ and 0.18 moles of OH-, and as the reaction between H+ and OH- is a simple one-to-one consummation to water, the excess is determined by subtraction of the lesser from the greater: moles of OH- in excess = 0.18 − 0.08 = 0.10 moles, whence it follows that hydroxide remains in surplus after the mutual neutralisation of the strong species.

Yet one must not neglect the acetic acid; being a weak acid, it might be thought to supply further protons, but in the presence of the excess strong base those protons will be abstracted until the weak acid is converted into its conjugate base. Thus the subsequent step is to assess the extent to which the excess OH- is consumed by CH3COOH.

The acetic acid, in the quantity of 500 mL at 0.1 M, yields moles of CH3COOH equal to 0.5 L × 0.1 mol L^-1 = 0.05 moles. The reaction of deprotonation, written CH3COOH + OH- → CH3COO- + H2O, proceeds in a one-to-one fashion; seeing that the excess OH- is 0.10 moles while the CH3COOH supplies only 0.05 moles to be neutralised, the OH- will consume the entire acetic acid and nevertheless remain in excess by the difference 0.10 − 0.05 = 0.05 moles.

Consequently, after all neutralisation is complete, the solution contains 0.05 moles of free OH-; to determine the pH we require its molar concentration, which is found by dividing by the total volume, 1.2 L, giving [OH-] = 0.05 mol / 1.2 L = 0.041666... M.

One now computes the pOH as the negative base-ten logarithm of this concentration: pOH = −log[OH-] = −log(0.041666...), and for the purposes of arithmetic one may note that 0.041666 is 4.1666 × 10^-2, whence log(0.041666) = log(4.1666) + log(10^-2) ≈ 0.6198 − 2 = −1.3802; therefore pOH ≈ 1.3802. Finally, since pH + pOH = 14 under customary conditions, one obtains pH = 14 − pOH = 14 − 1.3802 ≈ 12.6198, which, when expressed to the precision of the offered choices, is approximately 12.62.

All of the preceding arithmetic and chemical reasoning being thus consistent and complete, one concludes that the correct choice is B) 12.62.

Let us proceed to address this enquiry with deliberate care. The question demands, with singular clarity, the identification of that assertion concerning post-transcriptional processes which is the least correct, and presents four alternatives designated A, B, C, and D.

First, one must recall, as a matter of elementary doctrine, what the phrase post-transcriptional processes denotes; namely, those several modifications which befall an RNA molecule after it hath been transcribed from the DNA template, and which include, among other operations, the excision of introns by splicing, the addition of a 5′ cap, the affixation of a polyadenylate tail, and sundry other steps of molecular processing; with this preliminary recollection before us, we shall examine the several alternatives in order.

Concerning Option A, it is asserted that upon occasion the segment of RNA corresponding to an intron is capable of excising itself in the absence of the spliceosome; one remembers that introns are the non-coding intervals of a primary transcript, and that the canonical mechanism of their removal implieth the spliceosomal apparatus which expunges introns and conjoins exons; yet it is most curious and true that there exist introns, of the group I and group II varieties, which possess intrinsic catalytic power and are able, without the intervention of the spliceosome, to accomplish their own removal; hence one is inclined to regard A as a correct statement.

Turning to Option B, the proposition is offered that in animals the introns present in the primary messenger RNA for canonical histones are excised within the nucleus. One observes that histones are the proteins which contribute to the packaging of DNA, and one recollects, with some perturbation, that histone mRNAs in animals display peculiarities of processing; doubt arises, therefore, for if the canonical histone genes in mammals and many animals are characteristically devoid of introns, then there would be no introns to be removed, and the generalisation that introns are removed in the nucleus would be inapplicable in that particular context. Yet one hesitates, for it is conceivable that in some organisms histone genes do contain introns and that such introns would, as with other pre-mRNA introns, be excised in the nuclear compartment: thus the truth of B depends upon the precise biological particulars, and one confesses some uncertainty as to whether the canonical histone primary transcripts of animals uniformly contain introns or are generally intronless.

With respect to Option C, the statement that a mature messenger RNA may present itself in alternative combinations of exons is precisely the doctrine of alternative splicing, whereby different exon combinations are included or omitted to give rise to distinct mature transcripts; this is a well established phenomenon, and hence one must pronounce C to be correct.

Option D affirmeth that certain histone mRNAs terminate in a stem-loop structure rather than a poly-A tail; this peculiarity of animal histone mRNAs is well attested in the literature, and one may therefore accept D as correct.

Returning to the perplexity which beset Option B, if, as one believes to be the case for canonical histone genes in mammals, the gene transcripts are commonly intronless, then the proposition that introns in those primary transcripts are removed in the nucleus is inapt, for there are no introns to remove; conversely, should there exist taxa in which histone genes do possess introns, then the statement would be true for those instances; yet, on balance, and in the light of the common intronless character of mammalian canonical histone genes, one is warranted in regarding B as the incorrect or least correct assertion among the four offered.

Thus, after weighing the foregoing considerations and acknowledging the small degree of doubt already expressed, the conclusion most consonant with the facts as I understand them is that Option B is the least correct statement.

Very well, let us consider the matter with due care. The problem before us concerns an absorption line, observed in radiation from objects at a cosmical distance of about 2.1 Gpc, whose energy equivalent is stated to be approximately 3.9 microelectronvolts, and we are to determine which phase of the interstellar medium within our own Galaxy would most readily produce such an absorption feature among the given alternatives of molecular or atomic, warm or cold.

First, one must recall the provenance of absorption lines in the interstellar medium: they arise from particular transitions of atoms or molecules inhabiting the various phases of the ISM, and the numerical magnitude of the photon energy in question, 3.9×10^-6 eV, is the datum upon which further inference must be grounded. It is prudent to examine whether this energy might correspond to a thermal energy scale or, alternatively, to a discrete radiative transition. The thermal energy per particle is typically expressed by kT, and if one were to attempt at once to equate the given energy with a temperature one would proceed by recalling that 1 eV corresponds to roughly 11600 K; thus a naive multiplication 3.9×10^-6 × 11600 would yield 3.9×11600 = 45 240, and, when multiplied by 10^-6, one obtains about 0.04524 K — an extremely low temperature indeed; this result inspires suspicion that some confusion lurks in the conversion, for one remembers that the precise conversion between energy in electronvolts and temperature in kelvins is given by the Boltzmann constant k ≈ 8.617×10^-5 eV/K, and therefore the more accurate relation T = E/k must be employed.

Hence, letting E = 3.9×10^-6 eV and k = 8.617×10^-5 eV/K, one obtains T ≈ (3.9×10^-6)/(8.617×10^-5) K ≈ 0.045 K, which, though extremely cold and indeed nearly at the limits of what one might imagine for an interstellar parcel, does not by itself command our final judgment, since the energy quoted in the problem more naturally denotes the energy of the absorbed photon rather than the kinetic thermal energy of the gas; in other words, one must attend to the fact that astronomical spectral lines are ordinarily associated with particular radiative transitions whose energies are fixed by quantum mechanics, and are not to be conflated with the thermal kinetic energies of the particles comprising the medium.

Thus, to place the photon energy on a more familiar footing, one may convert it into a wavelength via the relation λ = hc/E, bearing in mind that Planck's constant may be taken as h ≈ 4.135667696×10^-15 eV·s and the speed of light as c ≈ 3×10^8 m/s; substituting these values gives λ ≈ (4.135667696×10^-15 × 3×10^8)/3.9×10^-6 m ≈ (1.2407×10^-6 eV·m)/3.9×10^-6 eV ≈ 0.318 m — that is to say, roughly 0.3 metres, or about 31.8 centimetres — which one observes at once to be in the metre-scale radio regime and which the familiar literature identifies with the celebrated hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen, commonly known as the 21-centimetre line.

It is most curious that, though my rough arithmetic yields about 31.8 cm rather than precisely 21 cm, the intended identification is apparent: the energy given corresponds to the long-wavelength neutral hydrogen hyperfine transition that radio astronomers habitually exploit; this 21-cm line is, as one may note, the signature of atomic neutral hydrogen (HI), and thus intimates that the absorber is of atomic, rather than molecular, constitution.

One must now consider whether the relevant atomic hydrogen resides in the cold or the warm phase of the neutral medium. The cold neutral medium (CNM) typically exhibits temperatures of order tens to a few hundreds of kelvins (say, ≈50–100 K), whereas the warm neutral medium (WNM) is characterised by far higher temperatures (of order several thousand kelvins, perhaps 6000–10000 K); nevertheless, the energy of the photonic transition that produces the 21-cm line is fixed and independent of the thermal motions, which instead manifest themselves in the Doppler width of the line rather than its central energy. Thus the mere detection of the 21-cm absorption signifies neutral atomic hydrogen along the line of sight; yet observational experience teaches us that 21-cm absorption is most readily associated with the cold neutral medium, where the line is typically stronger owing to higher column densities and lower spin temperatures, whereas the warm neutral medium, though it too contains HI and may show the line in emission or in weaker absorption, is less commonly the provenance of strong 21-cm absorption features.

There is a momentary subtlety to be remarked: the objects being observed lie at a distance of about 2.1 Gpc, and one might wonder whether the absorption arises in the intervening intergalactic medium rather than in our own Galaxy; however, the problem as stated asks specifically which medium in the Milky Way would most likely produce the observed absorption line, and so one confines the consideration to the Galactic ISM, wherein the 21-cm transition of neutral hydrogen denotes the atomic phase, and observational proclivity favours the cold atomic medium as the principal source of conspicuous 21-cm absorption.

Consequently, weighing the foregoing considerations and the unmistakable identification of the photon energy with the neutral hydrogen hyperfine transition, one concludes that the most probable answer is D) Cold atomic interstellar medium.

Allow me, with due modesty, to endeavour to unravel this puzzle. The matter before us concerns quantum mechanics, as one readily discerns; we are presented with a system whose state vector at the time t is given by the column matrix (-1, 2, 1)^{T}, and two operators, P and Q, are specified; the question posed, if I understand it aright, is the probability of obtaining the outcome 0 upon measurement of P and subsequently obtaining the outcome -1 upon measurement of Q.

To proceed rightly, one must recall, as a fundamental rule, that for an observable the probability of a particular eigenvalue is the square of the absolute value of the projection of the state vector upon the corresponding eigenstate; yet, because here we have a succession of measurements, namely P followed by Q, we must further remember that the measurement of P effects a collapse of the state into an eigenstate of P, and the subsequent measurement of Q is performed upon that collapsed state.

Thus I shall proceed step by step, with such methodical care as the subject demands:

1. One must find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the operator P, for when P is measured the state will collapse into one of those eigenstates, and for the given initial state we may then compute the probability of each eigenvalue.

2. For each possible eigenstate of P one would compute the conditional probability of obtaining -1 for Q, and thereafter combine these probabilities by the ordinary rule of total probability; but, since the question specifically inquires after the joint event of P yielding 0 and then Q yielding -1, one needeth only the probability that P gives 0 and, having so given, the conditional probability that Q subsequently gives -1, and to multiply them together.

Before computing probabilities, therefore, let us set down the matrices of the operators in the clear fashion. The matrix for P is

Row 1: [0, 1/√2, 0]

Row 2: [1/√2, 0, 1/√2]

Row 3: [0, 1/√2, 0]

and the matrix for Q is

Row 1: [1, 0, 0]

Row 2: [0, 0, 0]

Row 3: [0, 0, -1].

The latter operator Q is diagonal, which greatly simplifies our task; its eigenvalues are 1, 0, and -1, with corresponding eigenvectors the standard basis vectors (1,0,0)^{T}, (0,1,0)^{T}, and (0,0,1)^{T}, respectively.

But, as was observed, we must first address P; the possible outcomes of P must be ascertained, and then for each such outcome one may inquire after the subsequent probability for Q. The question, to repeat, asks for the probability of getting 0 for P and -1 for Q; thus we seek the probability that P yields 0, multiplied by the probability that Q yields -1 given that collapse.

We must therefore obtain the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of P. It is perhaps worth remarking, before embarking upon the algebra, that P is plainly Hermitian, for all its elements are real and the matrix is symmetric; hence its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors may be chosen orthogonal. The matrix P may be written as

[ 0        1/√2      0     ]
[1/√2     0        1/√2  ]
[ 0       1/√2     0     ],

and the characteristic equation is det(P - λI) = 0. One might, in the ordinary course, expand this determinant; yet, as I hesitated and found that such an expansion threatened to be tedious, I turned my attention to the symmetry of the matrix, which suggests certain forms for the eigenvectors.

Noticing the symmetry between the first and third components, one may naturally trial an eigenvector of the form (a, b, a), whence upon multiplication by P one obtains the vector whose first component is b/√2, whose second component is √2 a, and whose third component is b/√2. For this to be an eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue λ we require b/√2 = λ a and √2 a = λ b, the first and third equations being identical; eliminating b by substitution, or combining these two conditions, one arrives at 1 = λ^{2}, whence λ = ±1.

Thus for λ = 1 the relation √2 a = b yields b = √2 a, and an eigenvector is (a, √2 a, a); taking a = 1 for convenience gives (1, √2, 1), whose norm squared is 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, whence the normalized eigenvector is (1/2, √2/2, 1/2). For λ = -1 one finds b = -√2 a and hence an eigenvector (1, -√2, 1), which likewise normalizes to (1/2, -√2/2, 1/2).

It remains to find the third eigenvalue; here one may invoke the trace of the matrix, which is 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, and since the sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace, and we have already discovered eigenvalues 1 and -1, the third eigenvalue must be 0. To obtain the corresponding eigenvector one solves P v = 0, which yields from the first and third rows (1/√2) v_{2} = 0 and from the second row (1/√2)(v_{1} + v_{3}) = 0, whence v_{2} = 0 and v_{1} = - v_{3}. Thus an eigenvector for eigenvalue 0 is (1, 0, -1); its norm squared is 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, and the normalized form is (1/√2, 0, -1/√2).

Summarizing, therefore, the three orthonormal eigenvectors of P are:

For λ = 1 : (1/2, √2/2, 1/2),

For λ = -1 : (1/2, -√2/2, 1/2),

For λ = 0 : (1/√2, 0, -1/√2).

We now turn to the given state, which I shall denote |ψ⟩ = (-1, 2, 1)^{T}; it is worth observing that this vector is not normalized, its norm squared being (-1)^{2} + 2^{2} + 1^{2} = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, so that the normalized state is |ψ_{norm}⟩ = (-1/√6, 2/√6, 1/√6)^{T}.

To compute the probability that a measurement of P yields the value 0, one takes the inner product of the normalized state with the normalized eigenvector of P corresponding to 0, namely (1/√2, 0, -1/√2), and squares the absolute value of that inner product. The inner product is

(-1/√6)*(1/√2) + (2/√6)*0 + (1/√6)*(-1/√2)

= -1/(√6 √2) - 1/(√6 √2)

= -2/(√6 √2).

Noting that √6 √2 = √12 = 2 √3, this expression simplifies to -1/√3, and the square of its absolute value is (1/√3)^{2} = 1/3. Hence the probability of measuring 0 for P is 1/3.

Once the outcome 0 for P has occurred, the state collapses to the eigenstate of P with eigenvalue 0, that is to say to the normalized vector (1/√2, 0, -1/√2). We must now determine the probability that a subsequent measurement of Q yields the value -1 when performed upon this collapsed state. Since Q is diagonal with eigenvector for -1 equal to (0, 0, 1), the required amplitude is the third component of the collapsed state, namely -1/√2, and the corresponding probability is the square of its modulus, |-1/√2|^{2} = 1/2.

Consequently, the joint probability of obtaining 0 for P and thereafter -1 for Q is the product of the probability that P yields 0 and the conditional probability that Q yields -1 given that collapse; that is (1/3) * (1/2) = 1/6. This accords with option D.

Very well, I must determine the ratio of those stars whose inclinations lie between 45 and 90 degrees to those whose inclinations lie between 0 and 45 degrees, upon the assumption of an isotropic distribution; let us therefore proceed by careful consideration. An isotropic distribution, as one observes, implies uniformity in all directions upon the celestial sphere; yet one is compelled to pause and reflect upon the precise definition of inclination in the context at hand, for the term is employed in sundry fashions. One wonders, for example, whether inclination is measured with respect to the line of sight so that 0 degrees corresponds to face-on and 90 degrees to edge-on, or whether the converse obtains; indeed, the conventional usage in stellar and exoplanetary discourse often denotes the angle between the rotation axis (or orbital axis) and the line of sight, so that 0 degrees would place the axis along the line of sight and 90 degrees perpendicular thereto. It is perhaps of minor consequence for the calculation before us, yet one should note this ambiguity.

Assuming, then, the isotropy so posited, one infers that the distribution of inclination angles upon the sphere is not uniform in the angle itself, but rather uniform in solid angle; accordingly the probability density for the inclination θ is proportional to sinθ dθ, since the element of area on the sphere is sinθ dθ dφ, and thus the number of stars in any angular interval is governed by the integral of sinθ dθ over that interval. Hence the task reduces to computing the integrals of sinθ dθ over the ranges 0 to 45 degrees and 45 to 90 degrees and thereafter forming their ratio.

We recall that the integral of sinθ with respect to θ is -cosθ + C, whence the definite integral from a to b is given by -cos b + cos a. Converting degrees to radians for precision, one notes that 45 degrees is π/4 and 90 degrees is π/2. For the interval from 0 to π/4 the integral evaluates to -cos(π/4) + cos(0) = -√2/2 + 1, which numerically approximates to -0.7071 + 1 = 0.2929. For the interval from π/4 to π/2 the integral is -cos(π/2) + cos(π/4) = -0 + √2/2, yielding approximately 0.7071.

The ratio of the latter integral to the former is therefore 0.7071 divided by 0.2929, which computes to approximately 2.414, and which one may sensibly round to 2.4. Thus the ratio of the number of stars with inclinations between 45 and 90 degrees to those between 0 and 45 degrees, under the presumption of isotropy, is about 2.4, corresponding to option C; hence the correct answer is C.

Let us take up the matter with due deliberation. The question concerns a textile dye which emits light bearing an energy of 2.3393 electronvolts, and we are instructed to determine which hue of light is absorbed by the compound; the alternatives proffered are Blue, Violet, Red, or Yellow.

First, one recalls that the energy of light is related inversely to its wavelength, so that higher energy corresponds to the shorter wavelengths and, conversely, lower energy to the longer; the visible spectrum, as one may note, extends from roughly 1.5 eV to about 3.1 eV, corresponding, in the course from the lowest to the highest energies, to red through to violet. Yet, it is perhaps prudent to summon the precise relationship between energy and wavelength.

The formula which connects the photon energy E and its wavelength λ is E = hc/λ, where h denotes Planck's constant and c the speed of light; nevertheless, one may also employ the customary numerical relation E (in eV) = 1240 (eV·nm) / λ (in nm). It may be that an exact computation of wavelength is unnecessary for some purposes, but in the present instance clarity will be served by the numerical substitution, although I entertain the possibility that such calculation might be avoided by appeal to remembered approximate values.

Permit, therefore, a recapitulation of the approximate energetic domains of the several colours: red light possesses the lesser energies, in the neighbourhood of 1.8 to 2.0 eV; yellow occupies something like 2.1 to 2.4 eV; green lies higher yet, perhaps 2.4 to 2.7 eV; blue is in the region of 2.7 to 3.0 eV; and violet attains still larger energies, up to some 3.1 eV and beyond. Be it observed, however, that our emitted light bears the specific energy of 2.3393 eV, and at once one perceives a potential ambiguity in the present question.

It is necessary to address this ambiguity with care. When a substance absorbs a photon it becomes excited and may thereafter emit a photon of lesser energy by virtue of nonradiative dissipation — a phenomenon commonly termed the Stokes shift — and hence the energy of emission is frequently lower than that of absorption. Thus, the absorbed photon will generally possess a greater energy than the emitted one. In the present problem, however, the statement declares that the dye emits light of 2.3393 eV; whether one is to infer from this the precise colour absorbed is not entirely explicit. In the absence of information concerning any Stokes shift, one might either (a) assume for the sake of simplicity that the emitted and absorbed energies coincide, or (b) regard the emitted light as indicating the complementary hue to that which is absorbed, as often occurs in the appearance of coloured substances. This is, I confess, a point of confusion and demands elucidation.

Yet, let us proceed by direct numerical conversion of the cited energy to its accompanying wavelength, for such a course will at least reveal the hue of the emitted radiation and permit us thence to infer the complementary absorbed colour if that be the intended interpretation. Using the relation λ = 1240 / E, with E = 2.3393 eV, one obtains the wavelength thus:

1240 divided by 2.3393.

An approximation will suffice to render the matter intelligible: multiplying 2.3393 by 500 yields 1169.65, which falls short of 1240; a further multiplication by 30 gives 2.3393 × 30 = 70.179, and the sum 1169.65 + 70.179 = 1239.829, which is almost exactly 1240. It follows that 1240 / 2.3393 is approximately 530 nm. Hence the wavelength of the emitted light is about 530 nanometres, a region of the spectrum that one would characterise as green to greenish-yellow.

Consequently, the emitted light may be described as green-yellow in appearance. If, however, the question seeks the colour of light which the dye absorbs, and if one accepts the customary observation that the manifest colour of a substance corresponds to the complement of the light it absorbs, then the colour absorbed will be the complement of green (or greenish-yellow), namely red. I must again note the earlier caveat: strictly speaking, absorption energies are ordinarily greater than emission energies because of the Stokes shift, and without explicit knowledge of that shift one cannot with absolute rigour assert the absorbed energy from the emitted value; nevertheless, in the present multiple-choice context, and given the absence of a green alternative among the offered answers, the reasonable inference is that the dye absorbs red light.

Therefore, upon the foregoing reasoning, the proper selection among the choices presented is the third: Red.

Now, let us assay this question. The querent asketh why potassium hydrogen tartrate is insoluble in water yet dissolveth in acid and in base. They wouldst also know how to verify this by experiment. The choices are A to D.

First, I must recall what potassium hydrogen tartrate is. It is also called potassium bitartrate or cream of tartar. The structure of tartaric acid hath two carboxylic acid groups and two hydroxyl groups. When it becometh a potassium salt, perchance it is a single substitution, thus KHC4H4O6. The full double salt might be K2C4H4O6, which is potassium tartrate. Soft, yet I wonder whether the double acid and the full double salt be different forms or if the fully deprotonated form existeth.

The question declareth that the full double acid (mayhap the fully protonated form?) and the full double salt (fully deprotonated?) are soluble, yet potassium hydrogen tartrate is insoluble. Why doth this occur?

Potassium hydrogen tartrate is a single salt, meaning one of the acidic protons hath been neutralized. The solubility in water dependeth upon ionic interactions and the structure of the compound. If the potassium ion be chelated by the tartrate ion, forming a stable complex, that might lessen solubility, for the complex becometh more like a neutral entity. But in acid, the hydron doth protonate the tartrate, rendering it more soluble as ions. In base, perchance further deprotonation taketh place, yielding another soluble salt.

Looking upon the answer choices, they all toucheth on how the potassium ion is chelated. Option B speaketh of methyl chloride forming methyl ethers, which would prevent coordination. Option C mentioneth acetone forming a ketal. Option D suggesteth oxidation to ketones altering geometry. Option A speaketh of D or L forms and meso.

Hold: the question concerneth why the single salt be insoluble. The reason may be that the potassium is chelated in such wise that the complex is a self-contained unit, which is less soluble. Adding aught that preventeth chelation would render it more soluble. For example, if acetone be added to form a ketal (option C), that would convert the vicinal hydroxyls into ether-like groups, which cannot well coordinate with K+, and so the chelation would be broken, and the salt should become more soluble. If this be so, then option C provideth a means to verify the hypothesis. Likewise, oxidation unto ketones (option D) would also alter geometry and prevent chelation, yet such oxidation requireth reagents, and acetone itself is used for ketal formation rather than oxidation. Methyl chloride (option B) is not appropriate to make methyl ethers under mild conditions here.

Thus the original structure of tartrate hath two hydroxyl groups upon adjacent carbons (C2 and C3). If they be converted to a ketal with acetone, those hydroxyls become blocked and cannot coordinate K+. This would break the chelation, making the salt more soluble. Therefore, option C is the correct answer.

Let us then set about this enquiry with due methodical care. The enquirer demands an explanation for the curious insolubility of potassium hydrogen tartrate in water, despite the reported solubility of the fully protonated acid and of the fully neutralised tartrate salts, and furthermore seeks a practicable means of experimental verification; the alternatives presented are enumerated as A through D.

First, one must summon to mind the identity and constitution of the substance in question. Potassium hydrogen tartrate is commonly designated potassium bitartrate, and in familiar domestic practice is known as cream of tartar; the parent tartaric acid carries upon its skeleton two carboxylic acid functions together with two vicinal hydroxyl groups. When one proceeds to replace a single proton by potassium, one arrives at the stoichiometry commonly written KHC4H4O6, whereas the doubly neutralised salt might be represented as K2C4H4O6; there is a moment of hesitation as to nomenclature, yet the essential distinction is clear between the singly neutralised and the fully deprotonated species.

The question itself asserts that the fully protonated acid and the fully neutralised salt are soluble in water, while the intermediate potassium hydrogen tartrate is anomalously insoluble; whence arises this anomaly? The solubility of such ionic compounds in the aqueous medium depends upon the balance of ionic attractions and the disposition of the organic anion to engage in internal coordination; if the potassium cation is so embraced by the tartrate anion as to form a stable chelate in which the ion is in some measure sequestered within a cohesive, less polar entity, then the resulting lattice or aggregate will be less disposed to dissolution, and one may thereby account for the comparative insolubility.

Moreover, one may understand how the addition of acid or of alkali alters the scene: in an acid medium, the surplus of protons will serve to protonate those anionic or coordinating centres upon the tartrate, thereby disturbing the chelating arrangement and favouring the production of species more readily separated into solvated ions; conversely, in a sufficiently basic medium further deprotonation and conversion into alternative salt forms will ensue, again affording species which are more soluble. Thus the hypothesis of chelation as the operative cause accords well with the observed solubility behaviour upon acidification or alkalinisation.

Turning now to the offered alternatives, one observes that several propose means by which the coordinating hydroxyls might be rendered incapable of binding the potassium ion. Option B invokes methyl chloride as an agent to produce methyl ethers and thereby to prevent coordination; option C proposes the employment of acetone to form a ketal with the diol, with the immediate consequence that the alcohol functions can no longer interact with the metal; option D suggests oxidation of the alcohols to ketones, thereby altering the geometry and so impeding chelation. We must examine, with cautious discrimination, which of these suggestions would constitute a plausible experimental test of the chelation hypothesis under ordinary laboratory conditions.

It is most curious, and indeed instructive, that the reaction with acetone to afford an acetonide or ketal is a recognised method for temporarily protecting vicinal diols, converting them into an ether-like cyclic acetal which no longer offers lone pairs for coordination to a metal cation; if the insolubility of potassium hydrogen tartrate in water arises from the very participation of those hydroxyl groups in chelation, then the formation of such a ketal would be expected to abolish the chelating capacity and thus to render the potassium salt more amenable to dissolution. Let us, with due deliberation, consider the matter at hand. The astronomer in question desires to examine the H-alpha emission profile of an active galaxy; she has at her disposal four candidate galaxies, situated at distances of 1 Mpc, 7 Mpc, 70 Mpc, and 700 Mpc respectively; the inquiry is which of these she should select.

First, one must recall the nature of H-alpha emission. H-alpha is a particular spectral line situated in the red portion of the visible spectrum, produced when a hydrogen atom undergoes the transition from the third to the second principal energy level. Active galaxies, such as quasars or Seyfert galaxies, commonly exhibit strong emission lines, H-alpha among them, by reason of the intense energetic processes in their nuclei, for example accretion upon supermassive black holes.

Now, the crucial consideration is that of distance; for, the greater the distance of the galaxy, the larger will be its cosmological redshift, and consequently the more the observed wavelength of a given rest-frame line will be displaced to longer wavelengths. The H-alpha line, in its rest frame, lies at approximately 656.3 nm; the spectral coverage in the present instance is coincident with the Sloan "i" band, which occupies roughly the range 750–850 nm. Therefore, for H-alpha to be observable within the i band, the redshift must be such that 656.3 nm multiplied by (1 + z) falls between 750 nm and 850 nm.

We may compute the requisite redshift bounds. For the lower boundary of the i band at 750 nm one requires (1 + z) = 750 / 656.3 ≈ 1.143, whence z ≈ 0.143. For the upper boundary at 850 nm one requires (1 + z) = 850 / 656.3 ≈ 1.295, whence z ≈ 0.295. Thus the galaxy must possess a redshift in the approximate interval z ≈ 0.14–0.30 in order that H-alpha fall within the i band.

We must now relate the given distances to redshift; for modest redshifts the Hubble relation serves as an adequate approximation, namely z ≈ H0 * d / c, where H0 may be taken as about 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 and the speed of light c as 3 × 10^5 km s^-1. Let us compute in turn for each distance.

For d = 1 Mpc: z ≈ (70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 * 1 Mpc) / 3 × 10^5 km s^-1 = 70 / 3e5 ≈ 0.00023. This value lies far below the lower requisite bound of ≈0.14; correspondingly the observed H-alpha would be at 656.3*(1 + 0.00023) ≈ 656.3 nm, that is to say essentially unshifted from its rest wavelength and certainly too blue to reside in the i band.

For d = 7 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 7) / 3e5 = 490 / 3e5 ≈ 0.0016. This too is manifestly much smaller than ≈0.14; the H-alpha line would thus be at roughly 656.3*(1.0016) ≈ 657 nm, again well short of the i band commencement.

For d = 70 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 70) / 3e5 = 4900 / 3e5 ≈ 0.0163. The observed wavelength would then be 656.3*(1.0163) ≈ 656.3 + 656.3*0.0163 ≈ 656.3 + 10.68 ≈ 666.98 nm, still appreciably bluer than the lower limit of the i band at 750 nm.

For d = 700 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 700) / 3e5 = 49000 / 3e5 ≈ 0.163. The corresponding observed wavelength is 656.3*(1 + 0.163) ≈ 656.3 * 1.163; performing the arithmetic in convenient parts, 656.3 * 1.1 = 721.93 nm and 656.3 * 0.063 ≈ 41.35 nm, whose sum is approximately 721.93 + 41.35 ≈ 763.28 nm. This value lies comfortably within the i band range of 750–850 nm, and therefore the H-alpha line from a galaxy at 700 Mpc would be recorded within the spectral window available.

It is proper to remark, with appropriate modesty, that the use of Hubble's law is an approximation, and that for greater redshifts a more elaborate cosmological relation would be required; nevertheless, given the figures before us, the redshift estimated for 700 Mpc (z ≈ 0.163) is sufficiently small that the linear approximation remains serviceable for our purpose, and the central conclusion is unaffected.

Therefore, since only the galaxy at 700 Mpc produces an H-alpha line shifted into the Sloan i band while the others remain too near and hence too blue, the astronomer should choose the galaxy at 700 Mpc — option A.

Let us endeavour, with due industry, to unravel this enquiry. The task before us is to determine, from the given spectroscopic evidence — FTIR, proton NMR, and mass spectrometry — the most probable molecular formula for an unknown substance chosen from the quartet C6H12O, C6H10O, C6H10O2, and C6H12O2; I shall therefore proceed to examine each datum in succession, and to marshal the conclusions which may reasonably be drawn therefrom.

First, the FTIR spectrum exhibits a very broad absorption band centred about 3000 cm⁻¹; one observes at once that such a broad absorption in this region is most commonly characteristic of O–H stretching, as encountered in alcohols or in the more strongly hydrogen‑bonded carboxylic acids, and thus a hydroxyl functionality must be entertained as probable. In addition, there appear strong absorptions at c. 1700 and 1650 cm⁻¹; the band at 1700 cm⁻¹ is, by familiar experience, most typically due to a carbonyl (C=O) stretch, as in ketones, aldehydes, or carboxylic acids, whilst the feature at 1650 cm⁻¹ may be assigned either to a C=C double bond or, less likely in the present company, to an amide; since a carbonyl band is present nearby, one is tempted to suppose that the pair of absorptions may belong to a carboxylic acid, which concomitantly manifests a broad O–H stretch in the 3000–3500 cm⁻¹ region; yet one must not hastily exclude the possibility of an unsaturated carbonyl (an α,β‑unsaturated system) which would alter the precise frequencies.

Proceeding to the proton NMR, it is stated that resonances corresponding to vinyl hydrogens are observed; such vinyl signals are the unmistakable testimony of a C=C unit, and therefore a double bond is present in the constitution of the molecule, which, together with the carbonyl indicated by the FTIR, will influence the calculation of the molecule’s degree of unsaturation.

The mass spectrum presents a fragment ion at m/z = 45. One must consider what elemental composition might give rise to this value: for instance, an ethoxy cation C2H5O+ would have mass 2×12 + 5×1 + 16 = 24 + 5 + 16 = 45, a possibility consistent with cleavage adjacent to an oxygen; alternatively, the ion COOH+ (that is, the carboxyl fragment) would weigh C:12 + O×2:32 + H:1 = 12 + 32 + 1 = 45, which is precisely 45, and so the presence of a carboxylic acid group would be concordant with this spectral feature; I note these alternatives without deciding prematurely, though the latter assignment would harmonise well with the broad O–H and strong C=O absorptions already considered.

It will therefore prove instructive to examine the candidate formulas with respect to their degrees of unsaturation, calculated by the usual expression DoU = (2C + 2 − H − X + N)/2, wherein halogens and nitrogens are absent and may be neglected. For the formula A, C6H12O, one computes DoU = (2×6 + 2 − 12 − 0)/2 = (14 − 12)/2 = 1, which furnishes but one degree of unsaturation; yet the spectroscopic indications suggest both a carbonyl (one degree) and a carbon–carbon double bond (a second degree), and so a single degree of unsaturation would be insufficient to account for that pair of structural features, rendering A unlikely.

Turning to B, C6H10O2, DoU = (2×6 + 2 − 10)/2 = (14 − 10)/2 = 2; this value of two degrees of unsaturation would accommodate, without strain, a carbonyl (one degree) together with a C=C double bond (the second degree), and moreover the presence of two oxygens is comfortably compatible with a carboxylic acid functional group (COOH), which would account simultaneously for the broad O–H, the strong C=O, and the observed mass fragment at m/z 45 (if that be assigned to COOH or to a related oxygenated cation).

For completeness, one must also regard option C, C6H12O2, for which DoU = (2×6 + 2 − 12)/2 = (14 − 12)/2 = 1, again affording but a solitary degree of unsaturation; since the data indicate both a carbonyl and a C=C moiety, a single degree of unsaturation is again insufficient, and C therefore appears unlikely. Finally, option D, C6H10O, gives DoU = (2×6 + 2 − 10)/2 = (14 − 10)/2 = 2, matching the unsaturation count; nevertheless, the FTIR evidence for a broad O–H stretch suggests the presence of a hydroxyl group engaged in strong hydrogen bonding, as in a carboxylic acid, and an O count of unity, as in D, would preclude the existence of a carboxyl group (which requires two oxygens), so D is less persuasive in explaining the ensemble of spectral facts.

One may therefore propose a concrete constitution congruent with B: for example, a linear unsaturated monocarboxylic acid such as CH2=CH–CH2–CH2–CH2–COOH, which would present vinyl protons in the proton NMR, a broad O–H and a strong C=O in the FTIR, and could feasibly produce the m/z = 45 fragment attributable to the carboxyl moiety. If one enumerates the hydrogens in this structure explicitly, one finds the following account: the CH2= carbon contributes 2 hydrogens, the CH= carbon contributes 1 hydrogen, each of the three internal CH2 groups contributes 2 hydrogens apiece, and the COOH furnishes 1 hydrogen upon the hydroxyl, giving a total of 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10 hydrogens; the carbons tally to six, and the oxygens to two, thus yielding C6H10O2, which is indeed the formula B. The molecular weight of such a formula computes to 6×12 + 10×1 + 2×16 = 72 + 10 + 32 = 114, from which a fragment at m/z 45 is plausible by the loss of an appropriate neutral or by cleavage to yield an oxygenated cation of the indicated mass.

In contrast, the other candidate formulas either supply an insufficient number of degrees of unsaturation to account for both a carbonyl and a C=C, or else possess only a single oxygen and thereby fail to account for the broad O–H absorption ascribable to a carboxylic acid; accordingly, upon weighing all spectroscopic evidence and the simple arithmetic of composition, one finds that B, C6H10O2, is the most plausible assignment. Therefore, B is the correct choice.

Very well; let us endeavour to unravel this enigma. The question presented concerns which one of the four specified compounds will undergo oxidation to its respective aromatic form with the least favourable thermodynamic or kinetic predisposition, the compounds in question being variously substituted or annulated derivatives of benzo[c]cinnoline.

First, one must recall with care what is entailed by oxidation in such contexts, for it is by no means a triviality; ordinarily oxidation of hydrocarbon frameworks may involve rupture of double bonds or the incursion of oxygen, yet here the transformation at issue is the conversion of a dihydro derivative, which bears two additional hydrogens and therefore lacks full aromaticity in one ring, into the fully conjugated aromatic system; benzo[c]cinnoline, being a fused ring assembly, will regain aromaticity upon removal of those hydrogens, so the oxidising process in effect is a dehydrogenation to restore aromatic character. One must further observe that the facility of such an oxidation depends intimately upon the relative stabilities of the starting dihydro form and of the aromatic product, as well as upon the particular structural circumstances that either render the saturated ring comparatively stable or predispose it to relinquish hydrogen.

The crucial point, then, is the stability of the dihydro precursor; if the dihydro species is comparatively more stable, it follows that the energetic incentive for oxidation is diminished, whereas if the dihydro form is less stable, oxidation to the aromatic form will be more favourable. Thus oxidation will be less facile when the starting material enjoys enhanced stability, and more facile when that material suffers from strain or lack of conjugative stabilization.

Turning to the compounds in detail, one observes first: 5,6-dihydrobenzo[c]cinnoline, which contains saturation at positions 5 and 6 and which, upon dehydrogenation, would furnish the parent benzo[c]cinnoline; if the dihydro form be less stable then the oxidation will be more favourable, but contrariwise, if that dihydro form be stabilized then oxidation will be rendered less favourable.

The second specimen, 1,10-dimethyl-5,6-dihydrobenzo[c]cinnoline, resembles the first save for the presence of two methyl substituents; methyl substituents are customarily electron donating and may impart stabilisation to the framework by hyperconjugative or inductive effects, and thus one might plausibly infer that such substitution will elevate the stability of the dihydro species, thereby rendering its oxidation less favourable.

The third compound, 4,5-dihydronaphtho[8,1,2-cde]cinnoline, presents a different pattern of fusion, the naphtho element indicating a larger fused aromatic ensemble; here the dihydro character at positions 4 and 5 would be converted upon oxidation to the extended aromatic naphtho[cinnoline] system. It is reasonable to suppose that the larger fused aromatic assembly confers considerable conjugative stabilization upon the aromatic product, and accordingly the dihydro precursor, lacking that portion of aromaticity, might be relatively less stable and therefore more readily oxidised; yet one must not be rash, for the converse might obtain if the dihydro ring relieves strain in the larger system, rendering the starting material unusually stable.

The fourth example, 3,8-dimethyl-5,6-dihydrobenzo[c]cinnoline, is akin to the first save for methyl groups at the 3 and 8 positions, and once more one must reckon that such methyl substituents can stabilise the molecule, thereby diminishing the energetic favourability of dehydrogenation.

Hence the question reduces to which of these dihydro forms is the most stabilised and thereby least disposed to undergo oxidation; if methyl substituents indeed stabilise the saturated precursor, then the dimethyl derivatives, namely compounds (2) and (4), would appear to be less susceptible to oxidation than the unsubstituted (1) or the naphtho-fused (3).

Comparing (1) and (2) one may note that the presence of methyl groups in (2) is likely to confer additional stabilisation by means of hyperconjugation and inductive donation, and therefore the oxidation of (2) would be expected to be less favourable than that of (1). In like manner, compound (4) bearing methyl substituents would be anticipated to resist oxidation more than the unsubstituted parent, so that both (2) and (4) emerge as candidates for the least favourable oxidation.

To discriminate betwixt (2) and (4) one must attend to the positions of the methyl groups, for their influence depends upon proximity and conjugative relationship to the dihydro ring; if the methyls reside at positions remote from the site of dehydrogenation their stabilising influence may be attenuated, whereas if they occupy positions that enhance conjugative or hyperconjugative stabilisation of the saturated ring their effect will be magnified. Without an exacting structural analysis it is difficult to be certain, and thus one must admit a degree of uncertainty; nevertheless, the naphtho-fused compound (3), by virtue of the extended aromaticity of its oxidised product, is unlikely to be the least favourable to oxidation, for the direction of change there is towards a very stabilised aromatic system and thus the dihydro precursor will tend not to be unusually stabilised.

Consequently the least favourable oxidations are to be sought among the methylated derivatives (2) and (4), not among (1) or (3), and since one must ultimately select an answer from the offered alternatives A)3, B)1, C)4, and D)2, and having weighed the considerations hereinabove, one is compelled — albeit with some reservation — to select D)2. I shall therefore go with D)2.

Wal, reckon we best chew on this a spell. The astronomer’s fixin' to study the H-alpha emission profile of an active galaxy, and she’s got four contenders at distances of 1 Mpc, 7 Mpc, 70 Mpc, and 700 Mpc — which one ought she pick, y’all wonderin'.

First off, gotta remember what H-alpha is: it’s a particular spectral line in the red part of the visible spectrum, emitted when a hydrogen atom jumps from the third to the second energy level. Active galaxies, like quasars or Seyferts, tend to show strong emission lines, H-alpha included, on account of the ruckus in their nuclei — accretion disks round supermassive black holes and the like.

Now the crux o' the matter’s distance. The farther a galaxy sits out yonder, the more cosmological redshift swaggers its light to longer wavelengths. H-alpha’s rest wavelength is 656.3 nm, which lives in the red, but if a galaxy’s far enough its H-alpha can be shoved redder than that. The spectral coverage we got is the Sloan i band, mind you, so any H-alpha we wanna study must be redshifted into that i band.

The SDSS has five filters u, g, r, i, z, and the i band sits roughly around 750–850 nm. So for H-alpha to show up in i, the redshift z must make 656.3 nm * (1 + z) fall between about 750 and 850 nm.

Let’s figure the z bounds: for the i-band lower bound 750 nm, (1 + z) = 750 / 656.3 ≈ 1.143, so z ≈ 0.143. For the upper bound 850 nm, (1 + z) = 850 / 656.3 ≈ 1.295, so z ≈ 0.295. So the H-alpha has gotta be redshifted with z between ~0.14 and ~0.3 to lurk in the i band.

Next up, how do those Mpc distances relate to redshift? For small z we can use Hubble’s law as a good rough saddle: z ≈ H0 * d / c, with H0 ~ 70 km/s/Mpc. Let’s do the reckonin'.

Take H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc and c = 3e5 km/s. For d = 1 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 1) / 3e5 ≈ 70 / 300000 ≈ 0.00023. That’s tiny, far below 0.14, so the H-alpha would be about 656.3*(1 + 0.00023) ≈ 656.3 nm, still right where it started — visible red, but nowhere near the i band.

For d = 7 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 7) / 3e5 = 490 / 3e5 ≈ 0.0016. Still durn near zero; H-alpha ≈ 656.3*(1.0016) ≈ 657 nm, still too blue for the i band which kicks off near 750 nm.

For d = 70 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 70) / 3e5 = 4900 / 3e5 ≈ 0.0163. That stretches H-alpha a mite: 656.3*(1.0163) ≈ 656.3 + 656.3*0.0163 ≈ 656.3 + 10.68 ≈ 666.98 nm. Still in the visible red, but still shy of the i band.

Now for d = 700 Mpc: z ≈ (70 * 700) / 3e5 = 49000 / 3e5 ≈ 0.163. That’ll push H-alpha good and proper: 656.3*(1 + 0.163) = 656.3 * 1.163. Do the arithmetic: 656.3 * 1.1 = 721.93 nm, and 656.3 * 0.063 ≈ 41.35 nm, so total ≈ 721.93 + 41.35 ≈ 763.28 nm. That right there sits comfy inside the i band’s 750–850 nm spread.

So only the 700 Mpc galaxy has its H-alpha redshifted into the i band; the others are too close, their H-alpha remain too blue relative to the i coverage. Now, mind ye, distances and redshifts ain’t exact kin without pickin' a full cosmology, and Hubble’s law’s an approximation, but for these reckonings and z ~0.16 for 700 Mpc, the linear estimate’s decent enough.

Given all that — only the 700 Mpc object places H-alpha in the i band — so the astronomer should choose the galaxy at 700 Mpc, which is option A. Much obliged for followin' along, partner.

Let us proceed, step by deliberate step, to unravel this inquiry; the question requires the expectation value of the square of the momentum, ⟨p²⟩, for a particle whose wave function is given by Ψ(x) = (b² - x²) for −b ≤ x ≤ b and vanishes elsewhere, and we immediately note, with no small importance, that the wave function is not normalized and therefore demands our careful attention before any expectation may be properly ascribed.

First, one recalls, as a matter of formal principle, that the expectation value of an operator is obtained by integrating the product of the wave function, the operator, and the complex conjugate of the wave function; since our present Ψ(x) is real and admits no imaginary component, its complex conjugate coincides with Ψ(x) itself, and hence one would write ⟨p²⟩ = ∫ Ψ(x) (−ℏ² d²/dx² Ψ(x)) dx, subject, as ever, to the proviso that the state be normalized; moreover one must be careful with the signs, and therefore one reminds oneself that the momentum operator is p = −iℏ d/dx, whence p² = (−iℏ d/dx)² = −ℏ² d²/dx², so that the operator is indeed −ℏ² d²/dx² and the expectation may be expressed as ⟨p²⟩ = −ℏ² ∫ Ψ(x) d²Ψ/dx² dx.

Nevertheless, since the present Ψ is not normalized, prudence suggests that we either normalize it forthwith or else compute the unnormalized expectation and then divide by the normalization integral; indeed one observes that for an unnormalized wave function the correct formula is ⟨p²⟩ = [∫ Ψ(x) (−ℏ² d²Ψ/dx²) dx] / [∫ Ψ(x)² dx], and accordingly we shall compute both the numerator and the denominator with equal fidelity.

We commence with the normalization integral, which we shall denote by N = ∫_{−b}^{b} (b² − x²)² dx; expanding the square, (b² − x²)² = b^4 − 2 b² x² + x^4, and integrating term by term one finds: the integral of b^4 over x from −b to b is b^4[x]_{−b}^{b} = b^4(2b) = 2 b^5; the integral of −2 b² x² over the same symmetric limits is −2 b² ∫_{−b}^{b} x² dx = −2 b² · 2 · (b³/3) = −4 b^5/3, because x² is even; and the integral of x^4 from −b to b is 2 · (b^5/5) = 2 b^5/5. Adding these contributions yields

N = 2 b^5 − 4 b^5/3 + 2 b^5/5.

To combine these terms one expresses them upon a common denominator of 15, whence 2 b^5 = 30 b^5/15, −4 b^5/3 = −20 b^5/15, and 2 b^5/5 = 6 b^5/15, and therefore their sum is (30 − 20 + 6)/15 · b^5 = 16 b^5/15; thus we obtain the normalization integral N = (16/15) b^5, and one may remark that the normalization constant, were it required explicitly, would be the reciprocal of the square root of N, though for our present purpose the denominator of the expectation value will simply be N.

We now turn to the numerator, for which we require the second derivative of Ψ(x); differentiating once, dΨ/dx = −2 x, and differentiating a second time, d²Ψ/dx² = −2, a constant, which renders the subsequent integration surprisingly straightforward; applying the operator −ℏ² d²/dx² to Ψ(x) therefore yields −ℏ² · (−2) = 2 ℏ², and consequently the numerator becomes ∫_{−b}^{b} (b² − x²) · 2 ℏ² dx.

Factoring out the constant 2 ℏ², the numerator reduces to 2 ℏ² ∫_{−b}^{b} (b² − x²) dx; this integral, being of an even integrand, may be evaluated as twice the integral from 0 to b, or directly by primitive, for which one obtains ∫ (b² − x²) dx = b² x − x³/3, and hence upon evaluation between −b and b one finds at the upper limit b² b − b³/3 = b³ − b³/3 = 2 b³/3 and at the lower limit a corresponding −2 b³/3, whence the difference equals 4 b³/3. Thus the integral of (b² − x²) from −b to b is 4 b³/3, and multiplying by the factor 2 ℏ² yields the numerator 2 ℏ² · (4 b³/3) = 8 ℏ² b³/3.

We are now in a position to assemble the expectation value: ⟨p²⟩ = (8 ℏ² b³/3) / (16 b^5/15). Writing the quotient explicitly as (8/3) · (15/16) · ℏ² / b², one may simplify the numerical prefactor: (8 · 15)/(3 · 16) = 120/48 = 5/2, and therefore the result is ⟨p²⟩ = (5/2) ℏ² / b², which one may equivalently express as (5/2) (ℏ/b)².

For completeness and with due circumspection, one may reexamine the steps for possible sign or algebraic slips: the numerator arose because the second derivative of Ψ is −2 and the operator −ℏ² d²/dx² therefore produces +2 ℏ² when acting upon Ψ, leading to the integral of Ψ itself which was 4 b³/3, while the normalization integral had been found to be 16 b^5/15; the ensuing division indeed yields (5/2) ℏ² / b², and thus the correct choice from the offered alternatives is B, namely (5/2)(ℏ/b)²; one notes, with mild curiosity, that although this wave function is not an energy eigenstate of the infinite square well, whose eigenfunctions are sine functions, the arithmetic here is straightforward and coherent with the foregoing derivation.

Let us, if one may, commence with the simple declaration that my task is to determine the value of the constant a which appears in the stated wave function. The wave function is given in the form (a / sqrt(1 + x)) - 0.5i, and the particles are observed only upon the interval x = 1 to x = 3. One remembers, as is requisite, that for a wave function to be admissible it must be normalized; that is to say, the integral of the absolute square of the wave function over all space must equal unity.

Yet, before proceeding further, it is most curious to note the stipulation that none of the particles were found at x < 1 or x > 3; this indicates that the probability of locating the particle outside the closed interval [1,3] vanishes. We are therefore constrained to conclude that the wave function must be zero exterior to that interval, and hence the provided expression (a / sqrt(1 + x)) - 0.5i is to be understood as applicable only for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, and zero elsewhere. Thus, to effect normalization, one must integrate the squared modulus of ψ(x) across x from 1 to 3 and enforce that the result equals unity.

Let us write the function more plainly: ψ(x) = [a / sqrt(1 + x)] - 0.5i. It is manifest that this is a complex-valued function, and therefore the absolute square is given by the sum of the squares of its real and imaginary parts; specifically, |ψ(x)|² = [Re ψ]² + [Im ψ]².

Accordingly, the real part is a / sqrt(1 + x) whilst the imaginary part is -0.5, whence |ψ(x)|² = a²/(1 + x) + (0.5)², the latter term resulting from (-0.5)² = 0.25. Consequently, the normalization condition becomes the equality
∫_{1}^{3} [a²/(1 + x) + 0.25] dx = 1.

Permit then the division of the integral into two more tractable pieces:
∫_{1}^{3} a²/(1 + x) dx + ∫_{1}^{3} 0.25 dx = 1.

The first integral is a² times the integral of 1/(1 + x) with respect to x, and we recall the antiderivative of 1/(1 + x) to be ln|1 + x|; hence, when evaluated between the limits 1 and 3, it yields ln(4) - ln(2) = ln(4/2) = ln(2). Thus the first integral contributes a² ln(2).

The second integral is the product of the constant 0.25 by the length of the interval, namely (3 - 1) = 2, and therefore it equals 0.25 × 2 = 0.5.

Collecting these results, one arrives at the equation
a² ln(2) + 0.5 = 1.

From which it follows that
a² ln(2) = 0.5,
and therefore
a² = 0.5 / ln(2).

Taking the positive square root (as is conventional for the amplitude constant in this context), one obtains
a = sqrt(0.5 / ln(2)).

For numerical appraisal, we may recall that ln(2) ≈ 0.6931; thus 0.5 / 0.6931 ≈ 0.7213, and the square root of this quantity is approximately 0.849, which, when rounded to two significant figures, accords with 0.85.

We must therefore conclude, after the foregoing calculation and the check thereupon, that the correct choice among the options presented is B.

One must first set forth the nature of the problem: to determine the energy of those gamma-rays whose lifetimes, in consequence of their encounters with the cosmic microwave background, are curtailed by the process of annihilation into an electron–positron pair; the average energy of a CMB photon is stipulated as 10^-3 eV, and this datum shall be retained for our subsequent computation. 

It is a matter of recollection, and indeed of elementary importance, that for a photon to effect pair production upon collision with another photon there exists a threshold, for the process γγ → e⁺e⁻ requires that the combined energy suffice to create the rest mass of the electron and positron; the rest mass energy of the electron is approximately 0.511 MeV, whence the simple doubling gives a total rest energy of about 1.022 MeV — a point to be borne in mind even as one recognises that a more rigorous treatment demands the consideration of invariants in the centre-of-momentum frame. 

Accordingly, one resorts to the invariant quantity s, familiar from relativistic kinematics; if one contemplates, as is most reasonable for the attainment of the minimal threshold, a head‑on collision in which the photons travel in opposite directions, then the momenta are opposite and the algebra for two photons of energies E1 and E2 reduces to s = (E1 + E2)^2 − (p1 c + p2 c)^2, which, upon recognising for photons that E = pc and accounting for the opposite sense of the momenta, becomes s = (E1 + E2)^2 − (E1 − E2)^2. 

Expanding this expression one observes that (E1 + E2)^2 − (E1 − E2)^2 = [E1^2 + 2E1E2 + E2^2] − [E1^2 − 2E1E2 + E2^2] = 4 E1 E2, so that s = 4 E1 E2. 

The threshold for pair production is attained when s equals the square of the total rest energy of the pair, that is s = (2 m_e c^2)^2; substitution therefore yields 4 E1 E2 = (2 m_e c^2)^2, and on simplification one obtains the succinct relation E1 E2 = (m_e c^2)^2. 

Employing the given value for the CMB photon, E2 = 10^-3 eV, one thus finds E1 = (m_e c^2)^2 / E2. To evaluate this numerically, note that m_e c^2 = 0.511 MeV = 0.511 × 10^6 eV, whence (m_e c^2)^2 = (0.511 × 10^6 eV)^2 = 0.511^2 × 10^12 eV^2. Division by E2 = 10^-3 eV then gives E1 = 0.511^2 × 10^15 eV. 

Carrying the arithmetic further, 0.511^2 is approximately 0.261, so that E1 ≈ 0.261 × 10^15 eV = 2.61 × 10^14 eV; converting to the convenient unit GeV (1 GeV = 10^9 eV) we obtain E1 ≈ 2.61 × 10^5 GeV. 

A moment of reflection upon the geometry of collisions confirms that the head‑on scenario considered above indeed furnishes the minimal gamma‑ray energy required for pair production, for it yields the maximal invariant s; if the photons were to travel in the same direction the relative energy would be diminished and the requisite gamma energy would be higher, so that the present result is the pertinent threshold. 

Perusing the offered alternatives, one finds option D to state 2.6 × 10^5 GeV, which accords with the value just deduced; hence the correct choice is D.

This conclusion, however, appears incongruously small, and so we shall examine more intimately the arithmetic just advanced.

One must take care not to lose by a momentary oversight the fact that the total volume after dilution is 40 cm³, hence the total number of moles present is best calculated by reference to that total; indeed the correct tally of moles of acetic acid originally present in the undiluted 20.00 cm³ of 0.05 M solution is 0.05 M × 0.020 L = 0.001 moles, and this quantity is preserved upon dilution, so that after dilution the moles remain 0.001. A moment of reflection reveals the slip: one had earlier multiplied the post–dilution concentration by only 0.020 L instead of by the full 0.040 L; in truth 0.025 M × 0.040 L = 0.001 moles, consistent with the invariant nature of moles under mere dilution. Therefore the correct number of moles of acetic acid present is 0.001, and consequently the volume of 0.1 M NaOH required to neutralize that quantity is 0.001/0.1 = 0.01 L = 10.00 cm³. Thus the equivalence point is found, with due precision, at 10.00 cm³ of NaOH added. One notes with some satisfaction that this correction restores numerical harmony to the argument.

Having thus established the appropriate equivalence volume, we may proceed to the enquiry concerning the pH at twenty–five percent titration. Twenty–five percent of the equivalence volume of 10.00 cm³ is 2.50 cm³ of NaOH. Let us compute the moles of NaOH so added: converting to litres, 2.50 cm³ = 0.00250 L, and hence moles of NaOH added = 0.1 M × 0.00250 L = 0.000250 moles. The stoichiometric reaction being quantitative, these moles react with an equal number of moles of acetic acid. The initial moles of acetic acid, as we have just established, are 0.001 moles; after reaction the moles of acetic acid remaining equal 0.001 − 0.000250 = 0.000750 moles, whilst the moles of acetate (the conjugate base) produced amount to 0.000250 moles. The aggregate volume of the solution at this stage is 20.00 + 20.00 + 2.50 = 42.50 cm³, that is to say 0.04250 L.

From these figures one may determine the concentrations:

[CH3COOH] = 0.000750 / 0.04250 ≈ 0.01765 M,

[CH3COO−] = 0.000250 / 0.04250 ≈ 0.00588 M.

Recognizing that this mixture constitutes a buffer, the venerable Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is appropriate, namely

pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]).

We first compute pKa from the given Ka, for Ka = 1.85 × 10^−5. The pKa is −log(1.85 × 10^−5) ≈ 4.73, as may be seen by noting log(1.85) ≈ 0.267 and hence 5 − 0.267 = 4.733. pH ≈ 4.73 − 0.4771 ≈ 4.25.

This value of approximately 4.25 accords closely with the offered choice of 4.26 in the multiple–choice array, and so one may record that the pH at twenty–five percent titration is approximately 4.25.

We turn now to the pH at the equivalence point. At equivalence all the acetic acid has been transformed into acetate; the moles of acetate present are therefore the original 0.001 moles. The total volume at equivalence is the forty cubic centimetres of the diluted acid plus the ten cubic centimetres of NaOH, giving 50.00 cm³, or 0.050 L; hence the concentration of acetate is 0.001 / 0.050 = 0.02000 M. and the relevant equilibrium constant is Kb, which one may derive from the relation Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0 × 10^−14. Thus

First, one must summon to memory the character of the nearest-neighbor model. The nearest-neighbor base-pair model apportions the thermodynamic magnitudes — enthalpy, entropy, and free energy — for DNA or RNA duplex formation to the contributions arising from adjacent base pairs, and these magnitudes are commonly extracted from melting experiments in which the duplex is subjected to a rise of temperature while its denaturation is monitored; such melting profiles are obtained by calorimetric measurement of heat absorption or, alternately, by the change in ultraviolet absorbance. This recollection established, one notes that the question avers that bulk experiments harbour a limitation which afflicts the results even when experimental conditions are, in every instrumental respect, ideal; accordingly we shall scrutinise the offered alternatives.

With regard to option A: that the change in heat capacity is taken to be zero — one hesitates not to observe that in calorimetry the heat capacity is indeed a quantity of import, for it governs the heat exchanged as temperature varies; should the change in heat capacity, ΔCp, be set to zero, the algebra of analysis is made simpler, yet such an assumption may be injurious to fidelity if the heat capacity in truth undergoes alteration during the melting transition. I recall that in certain thermodynamic treatments the supposition ΔCp = 0 is invoked and that this simplification can occasion inaccuracies, since the heat capacity does commonly change across the melting process; nevertheless, one is not yet fully persuaded that this represents the principal limitation sought by the question.

Turning to option B: that the nearest-neighbor parameters are independent of temperature. It is customary that the NNBP parameters be presented as values at a reference temperature, often twenty-five degrees Celsius or some such standard, yet in the reality of physical chemistry these parameters may well bear a dependence upon temperature. If the model or the ensuing analysis presumes that they are invariant with T, then predictive errors will ensue when one extrapolates to other temperatures. One must, however, take heed that the parameters themselves are deduced from the experimental observations; therefore if the experimental analysis assumes temperature-independence, that assumption becomes propagated into the derived parameters — yet I remain uncertain whether this constitutes the foremost limitation intrinsic to the bulk experiments rather than a collateral modelling choice.

Consideration of option C: the impossibility of capturing heterogeneity in bulk experiments. It is manifest that bulk measurements yield averages over innumerable molecules, and that any heterogeneity of species, be it alternate conformations or impurities, will be subsumed into an ensemble mean; nonetheless the question specifies that the limitation persists even under ideal experimental circumstances, and if one were to suppose those circumstances ideal, one might also suppose that sample heterogeneity is absent; therefore it is arguable that while averaging is indeed a shortcoming of bulk methods, it may not be the particular defect alluded to here.

As for option D: that temperature oscillations in bulk calorimetry are of such magnitude as to obscure temperature dependence — if the apparatus were not ideal, such fluctuations would indeed introduce noise; yet the question expressly contemplates the limitation that remains under ideal conditions, and hence one may dismiss this complaint, since ideal calorimetric practice would minimise oscillations to a negligible degree.

Option E declares that temperature cannot be controlled in calorimetric experiments, a proposition that seems plainly contrary to the nature of such investigations, for differential scanning calorimetry and analogous methodologies presuppose and in practice achieve precise temperature control; thus this option appears untenable.

Returning to the principal candidates, one discerns that the central failing of the standard bulk melting analysis is the habitual recourse to simplifying assumptions concerning temperature dependence. One recalls that the customary method for extracting enthalpy and entropy from melting data often embraces the van ’t Hoff approach, which tacitly treats ΔH and ΔS as constants, equivalent to assuming ΔCp = 0; yet in honest nature the heat capacity change is seldom truly null, and when ΔCp is not zero the enthalpic and entropic terms vary with temperature, rendering the oversimplified analysis inexact. Nevertheless, the most direct and conventional statement of the experimental limitation is that the change in heat capacity is assumed to be zero, thus simplifying the mathematics but imparting systematic error.

This reasoning being made, one is led, with some confidence, to select option A.

First, one must recollect, as best memory permits, the meaning of the title in question; a voivode, as one observes in the histories of Central and Eastern Europe, was commonly a military and administrative dignity within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and subsequently the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, yet it is most curious that the term was not unknown in the Russian dominions, and therefore one may entertain the likelihood that the designation applied to a Russian military or gubernatorial office in Pskov; nevertheless, we must confess some uncertainty touching the precise functions in this particular instance.

Next, we shall take account of the chronological circumstances: the year 1700 falls within the opening phase of the Great Northern War (1700–1721), when the Russian realm was engaged in strenuous conflict with the Swedish crown, under Charles XII, and Pskov held an importance that rendered its command figure significant in military affairs; Ivan Ivanovich Golovin was, as I recollect, a Russian military leader and is thought to have had responsibility for the defence of Pskov against Swedish incursions.

We may further note that among the principal actors of that epoch was Peter the Great, the Tsar, who took an active part in military direction, yet the query before us concerns not the sovereign but rather the individual who assumed the voivodship after Golovin; it is necessary, therefore, to consider each provided candidate in turn.

A) Boris Petrovich Sheremetev — upon reflection, one remembers Sheremetev as a conspicuous Russian general and statesman, and one is aware that he was the son of Vasily Sheremetev, who himself had formerly held the voivodship of Pskov; yet it is uncertain whether the son, Boris, was the immediate successor to Golovin.

B) Peter Matveevich Apraksin — Apraksin figures in memory as a Russian admiral and general of note, engaged in wars with the Ottoman Porte and in later campaigns; his connexion with Pskov in the year 1700 is not manifest to my recollection.

C) Mikhail Mikhailovich Golitsyn — Golitsyn belonged to the noble house and occupied statesmanlike posts, though I am not inclined to assert that he was associated with the government of Pskov about this precise juncture; his activities were perhaps more closely allied to court politics.

D) Vasily Borisovich Bukhvostov — Bukhvostov is recalled as a general engaged in the Great Northern War, and I think he took part in the defence of Pskov; this renders him an object of interest as a plausible successor to Golovin.

E) Fyodor Yuryevich Romodanovsky — Romodanovsky, too, appears among the military commanders of that era and had involvement in actions against the Swedes, yet I do not confidently remember him filling the voivodship of Pskov at the time in question.

A moment of reflection upon the precise chronology is demanded: Golovin is thought to have been in command at Pskov during the siege of 1700 and, as my recollection serves, he fell during the defence of the city in that same year; if he perished or was removed in 1700, then the voivodship must, by necessity, have devolved upon another immediately thereafter, and my recollection inclines me to the belief that Vasily Borisovich Bukhvostov received that appointment; yet I admit that certainty eludes me, and the alternative that Peter Apraksin succeeded him remains not entirely impossible.

In another vein of consideration, the simple inspection of the names offers that Bukhvostov, option D, presents itself as a plausible candidate, though I do not assert this with unshaken confidence; I further recollect that Bukhvostov was later engaged at Narva in 1704, which is a separate circumstance that does not decisively confirm or deny his succession in 1700.

One may also entertain the hypothesis that Boris Sheremetev assumed the voivodship once more, for if Vasily Sheremetev had been voivode before Golovin and if dynastic or patronal influences persisted, the restoration of Sheremetev might have occurred; nevertheless, I incline to think that such a restoration is improbable in the present instance.

Accordingly, and with due reservation as to absolute certainty, I shall select D) Vasily Borisovich Bukhvostov.
