Very well, I shall endeavour to approach this inquiry concerning the constitution of a retroviral virion with deliberate care, and to state my reasoning in full; the question, as presented, requests a basic description of its structure, from among several enumerated alternatives, and therefore it is fitting first to recall the essential nature of retroviruses and of a virion as an independent entity.

One observes, as a matter of established fact, that retroviruses constitute a class of viruses whose hereditary material is comprised of ribonucleic acid, and that they have received the epithet “retro” because they employ the enzyme reverse transcriptase to convert that RNA into deoxyribonucleic acid upon entry into the organism they infect; nevertheless, the present inquiry concerns the virion, which is to say the complete viral particle when it exists external to the host cell.

It is requisite, therefore, to recollect the customary components of a typical virus: there is, in all cases, a genome, composed of either DNA or RNA; there is a capsid, a covering fashioned of protein which shields that genome; and in certain instances there is an envelope, a membranous bilayer of lipids which the virus derives from the host cell membrane at the moment of budding, an envelope which commonly bears upon its surface viral glycoproteins embedded therein.

Now, having recapitulated these considerations, let us proceed, with due method, to inspect the several options in turn.

Option A asserts the presence of a DNA genome, a protein capsid, and an inner lipid bilayer envelope; yet this proposition contradicts the primary fact that retroviruses possess RNA rather than DNA as their genetic substance, and moreover the viral envelope, when present, is ordinarily an external membrane rather than an inner bilayer; it follows, therefore, that A must be rejected.

Option B mentions an RNA genome, a carbohydrate capsid, and an outer protein bilayer envelope; but one must note that capsids are constructed of protein and not of carbohydrate, and that envelopes are lipid bilayers rather than protein bilayers; consequently B is erroneous.

Option C states that the virion is only RNA; such a simplicity cannot be sustained, for viruses characteristically include structural elements surrounding their genome, and thus C is incorrect.

Option D proposes an RNA genome, an outer carbohydrate bilayer envelope, and no capsid; again, this description errs in asserting a carbohydrate envelope in place of the lipid bilayer borne by enveloped viruses, and in denying the existence of a capsid which retroviruses possess; hence D is unsatisfactory.

Option E describes an RNA genome, a protein capsid, and an outer lipid envelope; this accords with the recollections above regarding retroviruses, which possess an RNA genome enclosed by a protein capsid and encased in a lipid bilayer acquired from the host cell membrane; this option therefore appears to be correct, though it is prudent to examine the remaining alternatives.

Option F recurs to the theme of a DNA genome, a carbohydrate capsid, and a lipid envelope; for the reasons already stated concerning genome type and capsid composition, F is incorrect.

Option G suggests a DNA genome, a lipid capsid, and a carbohydrate envelope; this likewise errs both in asserting DNA for a retrovirus and in ascribing lipid composition to the capsid and carbohydrate composition to the envelope, and thus G is untenable.

Option H posits RNA, a carbohydrate capsid, and an inner protein envelope; this again misconstrues the nature of the capsid and of the envelope, which in truth is a lipid bilayer bearing proteins externally, and so H must be dismissed.

Option I offers RNA, a lipid bilayer capsid, and an inner protein envelope; here too the roles of protein and lipid are transposed from their proper assignments, for the capsid is proteinaceous and the envelope lipidic, and therefore I is incorrect.

Option J seems to suggest a genome of protein; but since genetic information resides in nucleic acids, either DNA or RNA, and not in protein, J cannot be correct.

Returning, then, to the balance of probabilities and the facts rehearsed above, one may conclude that the proper description of the retroviral virion is that given in option E: it possesses an RNA genome, a protein capsid, and an outer lipid envelope; indeed, one may confirm from familiar exemplars such as the human immunodeficiency virus that this combination of RNA genome, proteinaceous capsid, and host-derived lipid envelope adorned with glycoproteins is characteristic, and therefore E is the correct answer.

Anon, let us assay this question. The question asketh wherefore the Treasury and the FED do commonly strive to lower long-term interest rates whilst they raise short-term rates. The choices be A through J.

First, I must bethink me of the offices of the Treasury and the FED. The Federal Reserve (the FED) hath charge of monetary policy, which includeth the setting of interest rates. The Treasury pertaineth more to fiscal policy, even government spending and taxation, yet at times they conspire together. Because the question nameth both, peradventure it concerneth their joint endeavour.

Now, why would they lower long-term rates and raise short-term rates? Let me muse upon the effects of interest rates. To lower long-term rates maketh borrowing cheaper for mortgages, business loans, and long-term investments. This can stimulate economic growth, for businesses may invest more and consumers purchase houses, which doth boost the economy. Contrariwise, to raise short-term rates (as the federal funds rate) maketh borrowing dearer for credit cards, short loans, and some corporate financing. This may brake inflation, for it reduceth consumer spending and short-term business investment.

Lo, if they raise short-term rates, that might check the economy. Yet the question saith they do this together with lowering long-term rates. Mayhap they seek a balance between stirring the economy (by low long-term rates) and preventing inflation (by high short-term rates). Yet I wist not if that be the exact cause.

Let us peruse the options one by one:

A) Lowering both promoteth borrowing and reduceth savings. But the question declareth they lower long-term and raise short-term. So A standeth wrong, for it argueth lowering both, which contradicteth the premise.

B) Raising both controlleth inflation. Yet again, the question saith they raise short-term and lower long-term. Thus B is incorrect.

C) Raising short-term encourageth domestic investment, lowering long-term leadeth to overheating. Nay; lowering long-term rates commonly stimu-lateth investment rather than causeth overheating. Overheating cometh of rates set too low, fostering excessive growth. This choice seemeth not to fit.

D) Interest rates have no effect. Verily, this is false; therefore D is wrong.

E) Lowering long-term increaseth the money supply, raising short-term preventeth bubbles. Lowering long-term may encourage borrowing and thus raise money supply by means such as quantitative easing; and raising short-term may slow lending to avert bubbles. This hath plausibility; I shall mark it for further thought.

F) Raising long-term discourageth the domestic economy. The question saith they lower long-term rates, so F is not relevant.

G) Lowering short-term stimulateth exports, raising long-term stabilizeth the currency. The question concerneth lowering long-term and raising short-term, so G setteth the converse and seemeth not apt.

H) Lowering long-term stimulateth the domestic economy, raising short-term encourageth foreign investment. How doth raising short-term rates encourage foreign investment? Higher short-term yields may allure foreign investors seeking greater returns. Meanwhile lower long-term rates maketh it cheaper for domestic firms to borrow for long projects, thus stimulating the economy. This combination hath sense.

I) Lowering long-term discourageth savings, raising short-term increaseth inflation. Lowering long-term would make saving less alluring, true enough, but raising short-term rates would ordinarily calm inflation, not raise it. Thus I is likely false.

J) Lowering short-term discourageth foreign investment. Yet the question saith they raise short-term rates. So J speaketh of the opposite and is not germane.

Thus the contest remaineth 'twixt E and H. Consider once more. The FED most oft useth short-term rates (the federal funds rate) to govern inflation. To lower long-term rates one may resort to other measures, e'en to buying long-term bonds (quantitative easing), which lowereth their yields. Such purchases inject money into the economy, increasing the money supply, as E saith. Raising short-term rates serveth to cool inflation and may prevent bubbles by making lending dearer. Yet H proposeth that raising short-term rates also attracteth foreign capital, for higher short-term returns do make the dollar more tempting; whilst lower long-term rates foster domestic long-run investment by cheapening loans.

Another view: raising short-term rates strengtheneth the currency and draweth foreign investors seeking yield, whereas lowering long-term rates encourageth domestic enterprise. Both E and H hold some truth: E noteth the money-supply effect of QE and bubble-prevention by higher short-term rates; H noteth the stimulation of domestic economy by cheap long-term credit and the attraction of foreign finance by higher short-term returns.

Methinks, upon weighing the matter, H best fit the question's framing. Lowering long-term interest rates doth stimulate the domestic economy by making long-term borrowing cheaper, and raising short-term rates doth encourage foreign investment by offering higher short-term returns and by strengthening the currency. Therefore I judge that the most accurate answer is H; I shall choose H.

Let us, then, endeavour to unravel this inquiry. The question propounds itself as an enquiry into the reason why the Treasury and the Federal Reserve commonly pursue the policy of depressing long-term interest rates whilst at the same time elevating short-term rates, and it presents options lettered from A through J for our consideration.

First, one must summon to mind the distinct offices and functions of the Treasury and the Federal Reserve; the Federal Reserve is charged with the conduct of monetary policy, of which the setting of interest rates is a principal instrument, whereas the Treasury pertains more immediately to fiscal matters, such as public expenditure and taxation; nevertheless, since the question names both authorities, it is plausible that the spirit of the question contemplates their conjoint effects upon the economy.

One may next ponder why one would wish to reduce long-term rates whilst increasing short-term ones. If long-term rates are lowered, borrowing becomes less burdensome for purposes such as mortgages, business capital outlays, and other investments of a durable character, and thereby such a reduction may serve to stimulate economic activity by enabling greater business investment and household acquisition of dwellings, which latter phenomena tend to quicken the economic pulse; conversely, an augmentation of short-term rates — for example, of the federal funds rate — renders short-term credit more costly, and by that mechanism may restrain consumer expenditure and short-lived speculative ventures, thereby exerting a cooling influence upon inflationary pressures.

A moment’s reflection suggests an apparent tension: to raise short-term rates is to retard the economy, yet to lower long-term rates is to encourage it; therefore the policy must be intended to strike some balance between stimulation and restraint, though the precise motive remains to be ascertained.

We shall now pass in orderly fashion through the offered alternatives. Option A asserts that lowering both long- and short-term rates promotes borrowing and reduces saving; this is plainly at variance with the premise of the question, which states that long-term rates are lowered whilst short-term rates are raised, so A cannot be correct. Option B posits that raising both serves to control inflation; again this contradicts the given pattern of opposite movements and must be rejected. Option C suggests that raising short-term rates encourages domestic investment while lowering long-term rates leads to overheating; this is an inversion of the customary effect, for lowering long-term rates ordinarily stimulates investment rather than produces overheating in itself, and therefore C appears implausible. Option D, which declares that interest rates have no effect, is manifestly untenable. Option E proposes that lowering long-term rates augments the money supply and that raising short-term rates prevents bubbles; this is not without some plausibility, for the lowering of long-term yields frequently results from central bank purchases of long-dated securities (quantitative easing) which does inject liquidity, and higher short-term rates may indeed act to check excessive lending, so E demands further consideration. Option F, which speaks of raising long-term rates discouraging the domestic economy, misdescribes the situation set forth in the question and is therefore not relevant. Option G, which asserts that lowering short-term rates stimulates exports and raising long-term rates stabilizes the currency, again inverts the movements described and so cannot be the answer. Option H avers that lowering long-term rates stimulates the domestic economy while raising short-term rates attracts foreign investment; one observes that the first clause accords with ordinary economic doctrine, and the second is defensible since higher short-term yields may draw foreign capital seeking superior short-term returns, so H presents itself as coherent. Option I declares that lowering long-term rates discourages saving while raising short-term rates increases inflation; the second claim is contrary to expectation, for higher short-term rates typically tend to diminish inflation rather than enhance it, hence I is unlikely. Option J speaks of lowering short-term rates discouraging foreign investment, but the factual pattern in the question involves a rise in short-term rates and so J is not applicable.

Thus the contest seems to come down to E and H. One may inspect E with care: lowering long-term rates can indeed increase the money supply when effected by purchases of long-term securities, and the elevation of short-term rates may serve to temper the formation of asset bubbles; yet H strikes one as more directly descriptive of the twin aims that one often reads in economic commentary — namely, that the reduction of long-term rates is designed to render long-term borrowing cheap and thereby spur domestic investment, whereas the elevation of short-term rates renders short-term financial instruments more remunerative and thus tends to attract foreign capital into such instruments and to support the currency.

Weighing these considerations, and acknowledging the plausibility of both accounts, one is led, with due modesty, to prefer option H as the clearest encapsulation of the rationale: lowering long-term rates to stimulate the domestic economy and raising short-term rates to encourage foreign investment.

Let us then begin this enquiry with due deliberation; the question set before us requests one to determine which among the enumerated conditions doth give rise to that clinical phenomenon known as female pseudohermaphroditism, and it will serve us to recall forthwith the nature of the term in question: pseudohermaphroditism, as one remembers, denotes a state in which the genetic sex of the individual is not in concord with the appearance of the external genitalia, and, taken specifically, female pseudohermaphroditism signifies an individual whose karyotype is female (XX) yet who manifesteth certain male-like features of the external genitalia.

We shall now proceed to examine the offered alternatives in succession.

Option A: Klinefelter syndrome. I conceive that Klinefelter denotes the condition in which an individual possesseth an XXY karyotype; that condition is commonly regarded as male pseudohermaphroditism because the subject is, by chromosomal account, male (XY) yet displayeth underdeveloped testes and may exhibit feminine characteristics; therefore, one judges this not to be the instance of female pseudohermaphroditism, and thus probably not A.

Option B: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). CAH is a collective of hereditary disorders affecting the adrenal glands; one remembereth that, in females, CAH may lead to an overproduction of androgens, and such excess hormonally induced virilization can occasion ambiguous or masculinized genitalia at birth whilst the karyotype remaineth XX; this circumstance accordeth with the definition of female pseudohermaphroditism, and accordingly B presenteth itself as a plausible candidate.

Option C: Graves disease. This ailment is an autoimmune malady producing an hyperthyroid state; one is not aware of any necessary connexion between this disorder and the development of genitalia, and thus C is improbable.

Option D: Turner syndrome. Turner is the X0 condition, wherein the person possesseth a single X chromosome; such individuals are ordinarily female but suffer from gonadal dysgenesis and related features; their external genitalia, however, are generally female, though pubertal development may be impaired; I do not conceive Turner syndrome to be a cause of pseudohermaphroditism, and hence D seems unlikely.

Option E: Campomelic dysplasia. I recall that this rare genetic malady chiefly producesskeletal deformities and at times sex reversal; I have in mind that it can lead to some individuals with an XX karyotype developing testes, yet I remain uncertain whether this presentation is classed as pseudohermaphroditism or as true hermaphroditism; thus E appeareth to be a possible but uncertain contender, and I must reflect further.

Option F: Androgen insensitivity. Consideration of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome remindeth us that such individuals harbour an XY karyotype yet are refractory to androgen action, whereby they develop female-appearing external genitalia notwithstanding the presence of testes; this situation is therefore an instance of male pseudohermaphroditism. One must pause, for the question concerneth female pseudohermaphroditism; if the subject were XX with some insensitivity to estrogens, one might be led astray, but no such common entity presenteth itself; perchance I am confusing matters; in truth, female pseudohermaphroditism describeth XX individuals with masculinized or ambiguous genitalia, whereas androgen insensitivity chiefly describeth XY individuals, so F is not the proper answer here.

Option G: Noonan syndrome. This disorder, which in certain respects resembleth Turner syndrome and arise from mutations in genes such as PTPN11, may produce cardiac defects, diminished stature, and occasionally ambiguous genitalia; yet I am not persuaded that it is a usual cause of female pseudohermaphroditism, and while it may in rare instances present with genital ambiguity, one thinketh it less likely than congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Option H: Marfan syndrome. This is a malady of the connective tissues and its manifestations are not typically concerned with genital development, so H may be set aside.

Option I: Prader-Willi syndrome. This condition chiefly affecteth appetite regulation and metabolic processes and is not ordinarily implicated in the formation or malformation of the external genitalia, so I exclude I.

Returning then to the most probable candidate, one finds B, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, to be the likeliest cause; in the female subject CAH provokeeth an overproduction of androgens with consequent virilization of the external genitalia whilst the chromosomal complement remaineth XX, which is precisely the classical circumstance of female pseudohermaphroditism.

I must, nevertheless, reexamine briefly the matter of option E, Campomelic dysplasia, for I recall that it can occasion sex reversal in some instances and that 46,XX individuals may, on occasion, develop testicular tissue, a phenomenon which might be construed as true hermaphroditism or ovotesticular development; yet pseudohermaphroditism, by definition, implieth that the gonads are of one sex whilst the external genitalia resemble those of the other, and if an XX individual beareth testes that situation would more properly be classed as true hermaphroditism rather than female pseudohermaphroditism; thus E is less fitting than B.

One further reflection: androgen insensitivity (option F) describeth an XY individual who presenteth female external genitalia despite the presence of testes, and therefore it is an exemplar of male pseudohermaphroditism rather than the converse; accordingly B remaineth the correct choice.

Very well; let us address this inquiry in an orderly fashion, and begin by recalling with some care what is signified by the term translocation in the vegetable kingdom. From my studies one recollects that translocation is the movement of nutrients, especially the sugars produced during the process of photosynthesis, from the leaves to other parts of the plant; it is the conveyance of organic compounds rather than of water, and therefore, when one considers the alternatives, it is necessary to distinguish it from those processes concerned chiefly with the ascent of water.

Addressing Option A, which asserts that translocation is the movement of water from the roots, one must at once dissent, for that phenomenon belongs more properly to transpiration and to xylem transport; water movement is usually effected through the xylem, whereas the transport of nutrients such as sugars is accomplished by the phloem; consequently A is incorrect.

Concerning Option B, which speaks of transfer of genetic material by grafting and by horizontal gene transfer, one observes that such matters pertain to gene flow rather than to the passage of nutritive substances, and therefore B is likewise inapplicable.

Option C states that translocation is the releasing of oxygen, which is an incident of photosynthesis; this again is a distinct process, for photosynthesis effects conversion of light into chemical energy and evolves oxygen as a byproduct rather than constituting translocation, and so C must be rejected.

For Option D, which enumerates capillary action, gravitropism, and phototropism, we may note that these phenomena relate to the motion of water and to the directional growth responses of the plant; capillary action may indeed assist in the movement of water but is not the mechanism of translocation of organic solutes, and therefore D is not correct.

Option E, which speaks of absorbing sunlight through the leaves, describes photosynthesis once more and not the movement of nutrients, and thus E is out of consideration.

With respect to Option F, which mentions the production of new shoots in the spring, one recognises that such a statement refers to growth and development rather than to the specific transport of sugars and other organic compounds, and accordingly F is erroneous.

Option G presents phloem loading, auxin transport, and electric potential; here one must observe that phloem loading is indeed a part of the translocation process, whereas auxin transport pertains more properly to the regulation of growth, and electric potentials may figure in certain hypotheses; yet one is not wholly certain that this grouping constitutes the principal theories of translocation, and therefore one remains doubtful as to the sufficiency of G.

Option H affirms that translocation is photosynthesis; this is plainly a confusion of terms, for photosynthesis is concerned with the synthesis of organic matter and the liberation of oxygen, while translocation denotes the subsequent movement of those synthesized substances, and hence H is incorrect.

Option I asserts that translocation is the movement of nutrients from leaves to other parts, and it adduces theories such as the pressure-flow hypothesis, cyclosis, and cytoplasmic tubules; this accords with the recollection already stated, for the pressure-flow theory is indeed the principal explanation remembered, cyclosis (that is, cytoplasmic streaming) has been proposed as contributory, and the notion of cytoplasmic tubules has likewise been advanced; thus I may well be correct in its definition and enumeration.

Option J, which lists diffusion, osmosis, and cellular respiration, must be examined with some care: diffusion and osmosis are indeed mechanisms of transport at the cellular level, whereas cellular respiration pertains to the production of energy and not expressly to theories of long-distance translocation; hence J does not offer a comprehensive account.

Accepting, then, that the correct definition is that given in Option I — the conveyance of nutrients from the leaves to other parts of the plant — one may briefly appraise the theories mentioned. The pressure-flow theory explains that sugars are actively loaded into the phloem, thereby creating a turgor pressure gradient which drives the mass flow of sap; its chief merit is that it satisfactorily accounts for bidirectional movement and has garnered considerable experimental support, though its weaknesses lie in the incomplete elucidation of the precise mechanisms of loading and unloading and of the detailed roles of companion cells. The cyclosis theory, which would attribute transport to cytoplasmic streaming, was once proposed but is now less favoured, for the structure of sieve tubes and the distances involved render such streaming an insufficient explanation; its weakness is the paucity of evidence and the difficulty of explaining efficient long-distance transport. The cytoplasmic tubules hypothesis bears resemblance to cyclosis in suggesting intracellular conduits for movement, yet it too remains less well supported than the pressure-flow account and does not enjoy the same empirical foundation.

All other options fail to define translocation correctly; therefore, upon consideration of the foregoing points and the evidence adduced, the answer must be I.

Let us proceed, with deliberate method and courteous attention, to examine this enquiry step by step; the question, as one observes, concerns the combustion of propane in one hundred per cent excess air, and it requires determination of (a) the dew‑point temperature of the products, and (b) the number of moles of H2O which will condense per mole of fuel when the products are cooled to twenty‑five degrees Celsius — a pair of inquiries for which the available multiple‑choice responses invite verification.

First, one recalls with convenience that one hundred per cent excess air signifies that the quantity of air supplied is twice the stoichiometric requirement for complete combustion; to establish a firm foundation, therefore, we write the stoichiometric combustion equation for propane:

C3H8 + 5 O2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O,

from which it is plain that one mole of propane consumes five moles of molecular oxygen at stoichiometry. Since ordinary air is approximately twenty‑one per cent oxygen and seventy‑nine per cent nitrogen by volume, the stoichiometric quantity of air, expressed in moles of air per mole of propane, is therefore

stoichiometric air = 5 / 0.21 ≈ 23.81 moles of air per mole of propane.

Given the stated one hundred per cent excess, the actual air supplied is twice this quantity, and thus

actual air = 2 × 23.81 ≈ 47.62 moles of air per mole of propane.

It is convenient to separate this total into its oxygen and nitrogen constituents: the oxygen present in the air amounts to 0.21 × 47.62 ≈ 10.00 moles of O2 (for, as one notes, 23.81 × 0.21 = 5 and doubling yields 10), whilst the nitrogen corresponds to 0.79 × 47.62 ≈ 37.62 moles of N2. Hence the combustion with excess air may be represented, in terms most explicit, as:

C3H8 + 10 O2 + 37.62 N2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O + 5 O2 (excess) + 37.62 N2,

for the stoichiometric consumption was five moles of O2 and the supply was ten moles, leaving five moles of oxygen in excess. Consequently, the product assemblage per mole of propane comprises 3 moles CO2, 4 moles H2O (vapour, initially), 5 moles O2 (excess), and 37.62 moles N2, giving a grand total of

total moles of products = 3 + 4 + 5 + 37.62 = 49.62 moles per mole of propane.

We now address part (a), the dew‑point temperature, by recognising that condensation commences when the partial pressure of water vapour in the gaseous mixture equals the saturated vapour pressure of water at that temperature. The partial pressure of H2O in the products is therefore the mole fraction of H2O multiplied by the total pressure (here stated as one hundred kilopascals), whence

PH2O = (moles of H2O / total moles of products) × 100 kPa = (4 / 49.62) × 100 kPa ≈ 8.06 kPa.

Thus the dew point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of water attains approximately 8.06 kPa. Recalling standard tabulated values of the vapour pressure of water, one notes that at forty degrees Celsius the vapour pressure is about 7.38 kPa, at forty‑five degrees it is about 9.59 kPa, and at fifty degrees it is about 12.35 kPa; since 8.06 kPa lies between the values at forty and forty‑five degrees, a simple linear interpolation furnishes the approximate temperature. The difference in vapour pressure between forty and forty‑five degrees is 2.21 kPa over 5 °C; the excess of 8.06 kPa above the forty‑degree value is 8.06 − 7.38 = 0.68 kPa, which is 0.68 / 2.21 ≈ 0.3077 of the interval, corresponding to 0.3077 × 5 °C ≈ 1.54 °C above forty degrees, and hence a dew‑point of approximately 41.54 °C — a value in very close agreement with the offered option E of 41.53 °C.

We turn, with like care, to part (b), that is, the moles of H2O which condense when the products are cooled to twenty‑five degrees Celsius. One assumes, as is customary in such treatments unless other specification is made, that the total pressure remains at 100 kPa while the temperature is lowered, and one recognises that at 25 °C the saturated vapour pressure of water is approximately 3.17 kPa; therefore the partial pressure of water vapour in the cooled mixture must be 3.17 kPa, and the remainder of the water will be condensed. Denoting by x the number of moles of H2O condensed per mole of fuel, the moles of H2O remaining in the vapour phase at 25 °C are (4 − x), and the total moles of gaseous products after condensation are (49.62 − x). Hence the condition on partial pressure is

[(4 − x) / (49.62 − x)] × 100 kPa = 3.17 kPa,

or, more compactly,

(4 − x) / (49.62 − x) = 0.0317.

Multiplying both sides by (49.62 − x) yields

4 − x = 0.0317 × (49.62 − x).

Evaluating the right hand side, one finds 0.0317 × 49.62 ≈ 1.572 and 0.0317 × (−x) = −0.0317 x, so that

4 − x ≈ 1.572 − 0.0317 x.

Bringing all terms to the left hand side gives

4 − x − 1.572 + 0.0317 x ≈ 0,

whence (4 − 1.572) − (1 − 0.0317) x ≈ 0, that is

2.428 − 0.9683 x ≈ 0.

Solving for x one obtains

x ≈ 2.428 / 0.9683 ≈ 2.51 moles,

so that approximately 2.51 moles of H2O condense per mole of propane (expressible, in the customary engineering notation, as 2.51 kmol H2O per kmol C3H8). This numerical result accords with the option E value of 2.51.

Therefore, upon the evidence and computation set forth above, one may conclude that the correct selection is E: a dew‑point of about 41.53 °C and condensation of approximately 2.51 kmol H2O per kmol C3H8.

Let us, then, proceed with deliberate attention. The problem before us concerns a three-dimensional harmonic oscillator, which is maintained in thermal equilibrium with a reservoir at temperature T, and our task is to ascertain the mean total energy of this system. One recalls, with some assurance, that in situations of this nature the equipartition theorem is the guiding principle; indeed, the equipartition theorem informs us that each independent quadratic degree of freedom in the energy furnishes an average contribution of one half kT to the energy.

We must next enquire how many such degrees of freedom are present in a three-dimensional harmonic oscillator. If one contemplates the motion in the three orthogonal directions x, y, and z, one observes that each direction supports not only kinetic energy but also potential energy; for each direction the kinetic term assumes the familiar form (1/2) m v^2 and the potential term the familiar form (1/2) k x^2. Consequently, for every spatial direction there exist two quadratic degrees of freedom, one kinetic and one potential, and, since there are three such directions, the total number of quadratic degrees of freedom is 3 times 2, yielding 6 in all.

Applying forthwith the equipartition dictum, and attributing to each of these six degrees of freedom an average of (1/2) kT, one obtains for the aggregate energy the product 6 times (1/2) kT, which simplifies to 3 kT; one thus arrives at the value 3 kT. It is instructive to verify this by an alternate phrasing: the total energy may be regarded as the sum of three kinetic contributions and three potential contributions, each contributing (1/2) kT on the average, so that one has 3 times (1/2) kT for the kinetic part and 3 times (1/2) kT for the potential part, these summing to 3 kT.

One must, to be candid, acknowledge that were one to treat the oscillator within the full quantum-mechanical formalism the mean energy would assume a different form; nevertheless, in the absence of any explicit quantum stipulation, and given the statement that the system is in thermal equilibrium with a reservoir at temperature T, it is most reasonable to employ the classical equipartition result. Hence the correct choice is E) 3 kT.

Let us now address, with deliberate attention and decorum, this inquiry concerning the differing modes of aquatic locomotion exhibited by the tuna and the dolphin; the alternatives presented extend from A to J, and I shall examine them in turn with the utmost care.

First, one observes that these two creatures, though both inhabitants of the sea, belong to distinct classes of vertebrate life: the tuna is a fish and the dolphin a mammal; this elementary distinction may, as one suspects, bear upon their respective modalities of motion. Permit me therefore to recall, with some specificity, the manner in which each proceeds through the water.

The tuna, like many of its piscine brethren, employs the coordinated action of body and tail, the muscular trunk contracting so as to drive water posteriorly; its caudal appendage is a puissant fin which oscillates from side to side, producing that undulatory propulsion which is the principal source of its forward thrust.

The dolphin, being a mammal and allied in habit to the great whales, presents a different organisation of locomotion: it propels itself chiefly by the action of its caudal flukes, which are disposed horizontally rather than vertically, and which move in an up-and-down plane; while the pectoral fins perform the office of steering and of maintaining equilibrium, the principal propulsive force remaining with the tail flukes.

With these recollections present, one may proceed to inspect the offered alternatives.

Consider D, which asserts that tuna swim by contracting their bodies and pushing water backward, whereas dolphins swim primarily by using their pectoral fins; here one must demur, for although the first clause concerning the tuna is tolerably correct, the latter clause misattributes to the pectoral fins the chief propulsive role in dolphins, whereas in truth the tail flukes supply the primary thrust; therefore D cannot be sustained.

Option I declares that in tuna the tail fin is oriented dorso-ventrally and moves side to side, while in dolphins the tail is oriented laterally with dorso-ventral movement, and it further avers that dolphins possess vestigial hind limbs and modified forelimbs for balance, whereas tuna lack such features; upon analysis this description accords with anatomical fact: the tuna’s caudal fin is indeed a vertical structure moved laterally, the dolphin’s tail is horizontal and oscillates dorsoventrally, and dolphins do exhibit vestiges of hind-limb structures and have pectoral forelimbs adapted for steering and balance, distinctions not shared by tuna; thus I appears to be accurate.

Let us, however, test the remaining alternatives briefly and with precision.

A proposes that both animals employ a side-to-side movement of the tail; this cannot be accepted, for the dolphin’s tail moves up and down, not laterally. B suggests that both utilise the dorsal fin for propulsion; this is a misapprehension, for dorsal fins chiefly afford stability rather than primary thrust. C would have the tuna employ gills for propulsion and the dolphin its blowhole for propulsive effect; such an assertion is manifestly erroneous, since gills and blowholes are respiratory rather than propulsive organs. E remarks that dolphins possess a flexible backbone distinct from that of tuna; yet all vertebrates possess spines, and this does not materially distinguish the modes of locomotion in the manner suggested. F alleges a spiral rotation of the dolphin’s body while the tuna flaps its fins; this is not consonant with ordinary observation of either creature’s principal mode of forward movement. G entertains the notion that tuna employ jet propulsion and that dolphins glide without active propulsion; both notions are misplaced, jet propulsion being characteristic of cephalopods rather than of teleost fish, and dolphins rely on muscular tail action rather than passive gliding alone. H asserts that dolphins use hind limbs; this is not correct in any functional sense, for external hind limbs are absent. J posits that tuna have modified forelimbs for balance comparable to those of dolphins; this is inaccurate, since tuna possess pectoral fins but not forelimbs modified in the mammalian sense for the purposes described.

Upon weighing these considerations, and having found the foregoing objections to the other alternatives persuasive, one is led, with a degree of confidence that I submit is reasonable, to the conclusion that option I is the sole statement which faithfully and comprehensively accords with anatomical and functional reality: the tuna’s vertical tail moved side to side contrasts with the dolphin’s horizontal tail moved up and down, and the dolphin’s forelimbs and vestigial hind-limb remnants serve roles in balance and steering that are absent in the tuna. Thus I is the correct choice.

We shall proceed to examine the question with deliberate care, for it concerns the determination of the electromotive force of a mechanical contrivance which conveys a charge through a region pervaded by an electric field, and one observes at the outset that "emf"—electromotive force—is, as one recalls from elementary electricity, essentially the potential or voltage furnished by a source, and is most usefully expressed as the work performed per unit charge; hence one may write ε = W/Q.

The problem, as stated, furnishes the magnitude of the electric field, the distance traversed, and the quantity of charge, and we must therefore connect these given particulars; it is most curious that the work effected by an electric field upon a charge in a uniform field may be expressed by W = q E d, where E denotes the field, d the distance, and q the charge; yet we must attend to the distinction whether this formula denotes work performed by the field or against it, because the device in the present instance conveys the charge and thus performs work against the field; consequently the emf sought is the work done by the device divided by the charge.

To make this explicit one may note that the force exerted upon the charge by the field is F = q E, and if the device is to move the charge opposite to that force it must apply an equal and contrary force; the work effected by the device is therefore W = F d, whence substituting F = q E gives W = q E d, and upon dividing by q one obtains ε = W/q = E d; thus, most satisfactorily, the emf reduces to the product of the field strength and the distance moved.

A verification by units is in order and will afford comfort: E bears units of newtons per coulomb, and d is in metres, so E d yields N/C × m = (N·m)/C = joules per coulomb, which indeed equals volts; thus the dimensional analysis confirms the expression.

Finally, applying the numerical data, one converts the stated distance of 20 centimetres to 0.2 metres, and noting that the electric field is 2 × 10^3 N/C (that is, 2000 N/C), one computes E d = 2000 N/C × 0.2 m = 400 volts; therefore the emf is 400 V, and upon inspection of the offered alternatives the correct selection is choice I.

Let us, without further delay, address the inquiry before us and marshal the recollections of our knowledge upon the subject of how intensity and frequency entwine in the perceptions of loudness and of pitch.

First, one must observe that loudness bears a relation to the intensity of the sound, that quantity habitually measured in decibels; higher intensity, as a general rule, produces the impression of greater loudness. Yet it is most curious that this is not the whole account, for frequency exerts its own influence upon our auditory sensibilities; we may note, with some assurance, that human hearing exhibits heightened sensitivity to frequencies in the neighbourhood of one thousand to five thousand hertz, so that tones in that band are perceived as louder than lower or higher tones of identical intensity. Hence loudness is not a simple function of intensity alone; frequency intrudes upon the matter.

Now, concerning pitch, it is determined by frequency: a higher frequency yields a higher pitch. One must also inquire whether intensity alters pitch; on reflection, one concludes that it does not. Even when a sound is rendered louder, its pitch remains constant; a shrill whistle, whether heard softly or with much force, retains its high pitch. Thus pitch and loudness are distinct perceptual qualities.

Turning now to the offered alternatives, let us examine them in order:

A) The statement that pitch and loudness are directly proportional strikes one as untenable, for the two attributes are separate in kind; therefore A is incorrect.

B) The claim that both decrease as intensity increases is contrary to experience, since increasing intensity ordinarily causes loudness to increase rather than to diminish; consequently B is incorrect.

C) The assertion that frequency has no effect on loudness contradicts the earlier observation that sensitivity varies with frequency, and so C is incorrect.

D) That perception of pitch is affected only by intensity cannot stand, for pitch is determined by frequency and not by intensity; hence D is incorrect.

E) The proposition that loudness depends upon both intensity and frequency, and that tones between one thousand and five thousand hertz are perceived as loudest, accords with the matters already rehearsed; thus E appears correct.

F) The brief assertion that loudness and pitch are independent contains an element of truth, yet it is imperative to note that E supplies a more precise and informative account; accordingly E is preferable.

G) The claim that loudness depends only upon intensity ignores the role of frequency and is therefore incorrect.

H) The remark that duration affects loudness is not germane to the present enquiry, which concerns intensity and frequency, and so H is irrelevant.

I) To say loudness depends solely on frequency is to neglect the principal role of intensity and is therefore incorrect.

J) The statement that frequency determines pitch while loudness is uniform across all frequencies contradicts the documented variability of loudness with frequency and is thus incorrect.

It follows, upon weighing these considerations, that the correct choice is E.

Very well; let us endeavour, with some deliberation, to proceed through this inquiry. The question presented concerns which among several statements, touching upon the digestion and absorption of protein, is most nearly correct; as there are many alternative propositions before us, one must first summon to mind the established facts regarding the manner in which protein is digested.

To begin with, one remembers that the digestion of protein commences within the stomach, where the enzyme pepsin performs its office, and where pepsin is derived from chief cells; yet a moment of caution is requisite, for the options set forth make reference to sundry enzymes and one must be precise. We must note, therefore, that the chief cells secrete the zymogen pepsinogen, which is afterwards activated into pepsin by the action of hydrochloric acid; thereafter, in the small intestine, the pancreatic secretions assume the principal burden, in the form of enzymes such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, and the carboxypeptidases. It is further to be observed that the enterocytes upon the intestinal brush border possess peptidases which contribute to the final degradation of peptides into constituent amino acids.

Having thus recalled the salient facts, we will now consider the offered alternatives in order.

A) The proposition that the products of protein digestion may be absorbed either as free amino acids or as dipeptides and tripeptides appears, upon reflection, to be correct, for one recollects that absorption may indeed occur in both forms, the di- and tripeptides often being conveyed into the cell and there further hydrolysed.

B) The statement that no brush-border enzymes are involved is manifestly incorrect, since, as was just noted, the brush border of the intestinal mucosa contains peptidases which assist in the breakdown of peptides.

C) The assertion that protein digestion occurs exclusively in the stomach cannot be sustained, seeing that pancreatic proteases within the small intestine play a major and indispensable role.

D) The claim that the products are absorbed by one of fourteen transporters must be questioned, for there exist several distinct transport systems for amino acids, and moreover dipeptides and tripeptides employ different uptake mechanisms — one may note, for example, specialised peptide transporters — so that the notion of a sole transporter among a specified fourteen is inaccurate.

E) The averment that gastric digestion is as efficient as intestinal digestion owing to antral grinding does not, upon consideration, commend itself; the stomach initiates digestion, but the small intestine, aided by pancreatic enzymes and brush-border activity, is chiefly responsible for efficiency, and the simple mechanical action of antral grinding is not sufficient to render gastric digestion equivalent in efficiency.

F) The statement that chief cells produce amylase is plainly erroneous, amylase being an enzyme of carbohydrate digestion, whereas chief cells furnish pepsinogen.

G) To assert that chief cells secrete chymotrypsin, trypsin, and carboxypeptidases is likewise false, these proteolytic enzymes being secreted by the pancreas rather than by gastric chief cells.

H) The proposition that gastric digestion is less efficient because of antral grinding is also untenable in the manner stated; if grinding has any effect it would be to facilitate breakdown, not to diminish efficiency, and in any case it is not the principal determinant of the relative efficiency of gastric versus intestinal digestion.

I) The declaration that all products use the same transporter is inaccurate, since distinct amino acids and peptide fragments are handled by different transport systems.

J) Finally, the contention that only dipeptides and tripeptides are absorbed is likewise false, for free amino acids are also absorbed directly.

Hence, having examined each alternative with some care and having weighed the physiological facts against the assertions set before us, one arrives at the conclusion that option A is the most correct: indeed, protein digestion yields products which may be absorbed either as free amino acids or as di- and tripeptides, the latter frequently being taken up intact and subsequently hydrolysed within the enterocyte. Thus A is correct, and the remaining alternatives contain errors or misstatements.

Let us proceed, then, to address this question of logic with due care, for the inquirer seeks to identify the species of fallacy contained in the argument presented, namely: "We must assume that he is a Communist, because he says that he is not, and we know that Communists are taught always to deny party membership."

First, one must dissect the argument into its constituent structure; the conclusion, as one observes, is that he is a Communist, while the premises are twofold: he denies being a Communist, and Communists are taught to deny their membership.

Translating this into the language of symbolic logic will, I hold, render the error most perspicuous. Let C denote the proposition "He is a Communist." Let D denote the proposition "He denies being a Communist." The premise offered amounts to the general claim that Communists are taught to deny their membership; hence, if one is a Communist (C), then one will deny it (D). Thus one obtains the conditional C → D.

Yet the argument, as given, proceeds thus: D is true (for he denies being a Communist); therefore C must be true. Here one discerns immediately that the move employed is the converse of the given implication. The original implication is C → D, whereas the argument treats this as if D → C were established; this is the very error commonly known in the treatises as affirming the consequent.

Permit me, however, to examine the alternative labels lest any doubt remain. A) Argument from Ignorance would obtain were the claimant to assert a truth merely because it had not been refuted, or the converse; that, however, is not the creature of the present reasoning, which does not appeal to lack of evidence but to a conditional rule about denials. C) Denying the Antecedent would present itself were the form "If C then D. Not C, therefore not D" in use; such is not our case. D) Begging the Question would obtain if the conclusion were smuggled into the premises as an unexamined assumption; yet here the premise gives only a conditional about behaviour, and does not simply assume the very proposition to be proved.

Therefore, having considered the structure and the foil options, one may conclude that the proper characterization is B) Affirming the Consequent.

Let us endeavour, with cautious attention to detail, to trace the proper pathway of visual information beginning at the very first station, namely the retinal receptor cells, which we recall are the rods and cones, and which one observes to transmit their impressions to the bipolar cells, whence in due course they pass to the ganglion cells; it is most curious that the axons of those ganglion cells, forming a compact fascicle, proceed thence to constitute the optic nerve. 

We must therefore note, and indeed we see with some plainness, that the initial step subsequent to the receptor cells is the bipolar and ganglion cell layers, and that the next stage is the optic nerve; from this nerve, as one is taught in anatomical description, the fibres proceed to the optic chiasm, that curious point at which the optic nerves from each eye cross over. 

After the optic nerve one accordingly meets the optic chiasm, and thence the optic tracts convey the visual impressions onward to the thalamus; the lateral geniculate body, which is a part of that great relay of the thalamus, performs the office of relay station; and from that lateral geniculate body the information is transmitted to the visual cortex situated in the occipital lobe. 

Having so enumerated the course, one may compare it with the offered alternatives: the correct sequence therefore should read — retina's receptor cells → bipolar and ganglion cell layers → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tracts → lateral geniculate body (visual center of the thalamus) → visual cortex.

Pray, let us proceed to consider the matter with the requisite care: the question asks why the aggregate demand curve slopes downward when the general price level rises, and offers options lettered A through F; one must determine which assertion is the correct explanation.

First, one recalls that the downward tilt of the aggregate demand curve derives from several well-known mechanisms, foremost among which is the interest rate effect, and it is to this effect that one gives immediate attention. When the price level ascends, households and merchants require a greater quantity of money to conduct the same volume of purchases and transactions, whereby the demand for money correspondingly increases; if the stock of money be fixed in the relevant interval, this augmented demand for liquid balances exerts upward pressure upon interest rates. As interest rates ascend, the cost of borrowing becomes heavier, and consequently investment and consumer expenditures upon durable and high-value items, such as dwellings and carriages, diminish; this contraction of spending reduces the aggregate quantity of goods and services demanded, and thus the negative slope of the aggregate demand schedule is manifest.

On inspecting the offered alternatives, one finds that option F affirms that the interest rate increases, which, upon the face of it, accords with the interest rate effect just described, and so appears prima facie to be the correct choice; nevertheless, prudence compels one to examine the remaining options in order to be certain.

Option A declares that the real quantity of money increases. Yet this cannot be so, for the real quantity of money is the nominal supply divided by the price level; when the price level is higher, a given nominal sum commands a lesser real quantity, and therefore A must be rejected.

Option B states that imports become relatively more expensive. Here one must pause, for an initial intuition might mislead; if the domestic price level rises while foreign prices remain unchanged, domestic commodities become dearer relative to foreign goods, and consumers will be inclined to purchase more imports rather than fewer, so that imports become relatively cheaper, not more expensive; hence B is incorrect.

Option C asserts that the value of cash increases. This is plainly contrary to fact, since a higher price level diminishes the real purchasing power of cash, and therefore C is untenable.

Option D avers that exports become relatively cheaper. On the contrary, when domestic prices rise, domestic goods offered abroad become dearer relative to foreign goods, so that exports become relatively more expensive, and D is false.

Option E proposes that the inflation rate decreases. Such a claim is inconsistent with the premise, for an increase in the price level corresponds to inflationary movement, not a reduction of the inflation rate; accordingly E is rejected.

Thus, having examined each alternative with deliberation, one finds that only option F, which states that the interest rate increases, accords with the well-known interest rate effect and hence is the correct answer.

Let us proceed to examine this question with due deliberation. The enquirer inquires concerning the consequences of castration upon sexual behaviour in primates of the highest order, when compared with creatures less elaborated — such as mice or birds — and from the statement furnished we learn that in those lower animals castration produces an almost total disappearance of sexual conduct. Having set this fact before us, we must now endeavour to compare it with the phenomena observable among the higher primates.

Proceeding to the several propositions, we shall consider them in turn with careful scrutiny.

Option A avers that, in superior primates such as man, castration does not affect the capacity to execute the sexual act if the individual be already mature and possessed of experience; upon encountering this assertion one is tempted to recall that in human history castration has been attended by a diminution of libido, yet perhaps the physical capacity to perform may persist; and one must further ask whether this circumstance implies that sexual behaviour itself is entirely extinguished, or merely that desire and performance are dissociated.

Option B pronounces that castration, when performed after the period of sexual maturity, diminishes aggression but does not affect sexual behaviour; this claim invites reflection, for if in lower animals the removal of gonads extinguishes sexual behaviour, it would seem plausible that the more complex primates might exhibit a less direct coupling between hormones and conduct; nevertheless certainty is lacking, and while in some primate cases castration may more notably attenuate aggression than sexual acts, one cannot be wholly confident without further evidence.

Option C proposes a transient decline in sexual behaviour followed by recovery, a notion which appears improbable upon reflection, for if the hormonal source be removed one would not readily anticipate spontaneous restoration of the prior state unless some compensatory physiological mechanism were present, of which I am not persuaded there is recall.

Option D declares that sexual behaviour is utterly abolished, which plainly contradicts familiar human instances, wherein castrated men often retain some sexual behaviour, albeit diminished; thus D appears untenable.

Option E, which asserts the utter absence of effect at any stage, strikes one as overbold and unsubtle, for even if behaviour be not wholly abolished one would expect at least some influence when the endocrine milieu is so materially altered.

Option F, which alleges an increase in sexual behaviour owing to hormonal imbalance, seems manifestly perverse, since castration removes the chief source of androgens such as testosterone, whereby one would anticipate diminution rather than augmentation of sexual impulse.

Option G states that castration affects the capacity in all animals alike, but this pronouncement is too sweeping; the stem of our problem asserts that in lower animals the behaviour disappears, and we are asked explicitly to compare this with primates, so a universal affirmation of identity across all species is not pertinent.

Option H avers that primates are incapable of acquiring sexual behaviour by experience, a proposition which is plainly at variance with observed primate learning and social acquisition of conduct, and may therefore be dismissed.

Option I suggests a permanent transition to non-sexual social behaviour; while some alterations in social interactions may ensue, it is by no means evident that such a complete and irrecoverable shift is the invariable consequence.

Option J affirms that castration before puberty prevents the development of sexual behaviour; this is indeed a true remark in its own right and accords with developmental endocrinology, yet it addresses a distinct temporal circumstance, whereas the present inquiry supposes castration in the adult and therefore J is not directly pertinent.

Thus, having narrowed our attention to the more plausible candidates, we are left chiefly to weigh A against B. The lower animals exhibit an almost total abrogation of sexual conduct following castration, whereas among primates the relation between hormonal presence and overt sexual acts is more intricate; historical and clinical recollections of castrated men show that while libido is commonly reduced, the physical performance of the act may remain possible in those advanced in maturity and experience, whereas B would assert that aggression is reduced but sexual behaviour is not affected at all, a claim which seems less consonant with the evidential impression that sexual desire in primates is nevertheless diminished, if not wholly extinguished.

Consequently, upon balancing these considerations, one is inclined to accept A as the most fitting response. Therefore, the answer would be A.

Let us now address this inquiry concerning buffer stocks within the agricultural market model, and proceed with deliberate care; first, one must recall the nature of buffer stocks themselves, and from my recollection they are reserves of agricultural produce which governments or organisations maintain with the avowed purpose of stabilising prices, for they buy surplus harvests when prices run low and, conversely, they sell from those reserves when prices rise, is that not so?

Turning our attention to the several alternatives presented, one must ascertain with exactness which statement truly characterises their importance, and so we shall consider them in orderly sequence.

Option A avers that buffer stocks eliminate the necessity for agricultural subsidies; such a proposition seems unsound, for though subsidies and buffer stocks may both serve as instruments of governmental policy, it does not follow that the latter wholly obviate the former, and perhaps they diminish the need but they do not abolish it, and thus we may reasonably reject A.

Option B asserts that buffer stocks result in price fluctuation; this claim appears to be the very opposite of the instrument’s professed purpose, for their raison d etre is the moderation and stabilisation of market prices, and if they were the source of volatility that would be contrary to expectation, whence B is likely erroneous.

Option C maintains that they ensure a constant decline in market price; such a statement is plainly untenable, for whilst the disposal of stock when prices are high might depress prices in the short term, the mechanism assures equilibrium rather than an unremitting fall, and therefore C cannot be correct.

Option D proposes that they provide farmers with unlimited income; the extravagance of the term unlimited renders the proposition manifestly implausible, for buffer stocks may serve to steady income but they can never confer an infinite revenue stream, and thus D is to be set aside.

Option E declares that they are primarily employed to control export of crops; I incline to think otherwise, for the predominant purpose is domestic price stability rather than the direct regulation of exports, and whilst indirect influence upon foreign trade may ensue, it is not the principal end, so E is improbable.

Option F contends that buffer stocks increase the price of crops; one must observe that their operations are bidirectional — the purchase of surplus reduces market supply and may raise prices, whereas the sale of stored grain augments supply and may depress prices — so their net effect is a tempering of extremes rather than an assured elevation of price, and hence F does not aptly capture their importance.

Option G suggests that they lead to overproduction and waste; it is indeed possible that the presence of a guaranteed buyer might induce excess cultivation and consequent waste, yet this consequence is a potential downside rather than the defining importance of buffer stocks, and therefore G is not the principal description sought.

Option H asserts that they stabilise the market price and impose no financial burden upon the government over the years; the first clause accords with the common understanding and indeed is correct, yet the second clause, which denies any fiscal burden, seems to be most curious and questionable, for the maintenance of reserves requires expenditure upon purchase, storage and management, and so one must doubt the absolute truth of that latter assertion.

Option I states that they are maintained without any impact on supply and demand; such an assertion is plainly false, for the very mechanism of buying and selling stock directly alters market supply and thereby affects demand relations, and I must therefore reject I.

Option J pronounces them to be a burden upon the government; it is true that costs of storage, administration and occasional losses may render them burdensome, but the question asks after their importance rather than their defect, and so J, though containing an element of truth, does not answer the query as to their principal purpose.

At this juncture one perceives that the essential object to be identified is the stabilisation of prices, and so we must determine which among these alternatives most closely embodies that truth; H contains the explicit declaration that they stabilise the market price, yet it appends the claim of imposing no governmental financial burden, which, as I have just noted, is dubious.

A careful reviewer might therefore hesitate, for none of the alternatives is without blemish; nonetheless, since the principal importance of buffer stocks is to steady market prices, and because H is the sole option that expressly affirms that stabilising function, albeit with an overconfident second clause, one is compelled by process of elimination and by fidelity to the central purpose to select H as the best answer, even though the assertion that no financial burden ensues is open to question; thus, having weighed each proposition and found them otherwise wanting, H must be chosen as the closest representation of the primary importance of buffer stocks.

First, one recalls that the energy of a photon is related to its wavelength by the venerable relation E = hc/λ, in which h denotes Planck's constant and c the speed of light; hence, upon rearrangement, the wavelength λ is given by λ = hc/E. We must, however, render the energy into the consistent units of joules, for Planck's constant h shall be taken as approximately 6.626 × 10^-34 J·s and the speed of light c as 3.00 × 10^8 m/s, whilst 1 eV corresponds to 1.602 × 10^-19 J. Substituting these quantities, one forms λ = (6.626e-34 J·s × 3.00e8 m/s) / (1.602e-19 J). Multiplying 6.626e-34 by 3.00e8 yields about 1.9878e-25 J·m, and dividing this by 1.602e-19 J gives approximately 1.24e-6 metres, which may more familiarly be expressed as 1240 nanometres; indeed, it is most customary to recall that hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, from which, for E = 1 eV, λ ≈ 1240 nm. One may therefore observe that the photon's wavelength lies in the neighbourhood of 1239.8–1240 nm, and thus the options presenting such a value merit attention.

Proceeding to the electron, we employ the de Broglie relation λ = h/p, wherein p denotes the particle's momentum, and for a non-relativistic electron (a presumption justified by the fact that 1 eV is vastly inferior to the electron rest energy of approximately 511 keV) the kinetic energy K relates to momentum according to K = p^2/(2m), whence p = sqrt(2mK) and consequently λ = h / sqrt(2mK). Adopting the electron mass m = 9.109 × 10^-31 kg and converting K = 1 eV to K = 1.602e-19 J, we evaluate 2mK as 2 × 9.109e-31 kg × 1.602e-19 J. The product 2 × 9.109e-31 equals 1.8218e-30 kg, and multiplying this by 1.602e-19 J yields approximately 2.918e-49 in the compound units (bearing in mind that a joule is kg·m^2/s^2, so that 2mK carries units which upon square-rooting produce momentum in kg·m/s, as is fitting). Taking the square root, one may compute sqrt(2.918e-49) ≈ sqrt(2.918) × 10^-24.5; since sqrt(2.918) is approximately 1.708 and 10^-24.5 may be expressed as 3.16e-25, their product gives a momentum p ≈ 5.40e-25 kg·m/s. Thereupon, with h = 6.626e-34 J·s, the de Broglie wavelength is λ = 6.626e-34 / 5.40e-25 ≈ 1.227e-9 metres, that is to say about 1.227 nanometres. This figure may be cross-checked against the convenient empirical formula for an electron, λ(nm) ≈ 1.226 / sqrt(K[eV]), which for K = 1 eV indeed returns λ ≈ 1.226 nm, thereby corroborating our preceding arithmetic.

With these determinations in hand — photon λ ≈ 1240 nm and electron λ ≈ 1.226–1.227 nm — one inspects the offered alternatives; one observes that option H provides Photon = 1239.8 nm and Electron = 1.226 nm, which accords with the values deduced above, whereas other contenders, for example the alternative giving the electron wavelength as 0.01239 nm, diverge markedly and may be dismissed. One electronvolt is 1.602 x 10^-19 joules. So pluggin' that in, λ = (6.626e-34 J·s * 3e8 m/s) / (1.602e-19 J).  
Multiplying 6.626e-34 by 3e8 gives about 1.9878e-25 J·m. Dividin' that by 1.602e-19 J gives roughly 1.24e-6 meters, which is 1240 nm — sure as shootin' familiar.  
By gum, folks often use hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, so with E=1 eV you get λ ≈ 1240 nm, so the photon's wavelength's about 1240 nm.

Now for that electron; since it's got kinetic energy we gotta use the de Broglie relation λ = h/p, where p's momentum, and with kinetic energy given we relate p to K.  
For non-relativistic electrons — and 1 eV's way less'n the electron rest energy of ~511 keV, so that's fine — K = p^2/(2m), so p = sqrt(2mK), and thus λ = h / sqrt(2mK).  
Plug in the numbers: electron mass m = 9.109 x 10^-31 kg, and K = 1 eV = 1.602e-19 J, so first compute 2mK: 2 * 9.109e-31 kg * 1.602e-19 J.  
Compute 2 * 9.109e-31 = 1.8218e-30 kg, and multiply by 1.602e-19 J gives about 2.918e-49 (units settlin' to kg^2·m^2/s^2 so the sqrt'll give kg·m/s for momentum, all proper).  
So sqrt(2mK) = sqrt(2.918e-49) ≈ sqrt(2.918) x 10^-24.5; sqrt(2.918) ≈ 1.708 and 10^-24.5 is 3.16e-25, so 1.708 * 3.16e-25 ≈ 5.40e-25 kg·m/s.  
Thus p ≈ 5.4e-25 kg·m/s. With h = 6.626e-34 J·s, λ = 6.626e-34 / 5.40e-25 ≈ 1.227e-9 meters, which is about 1.227 nm — right in the neighborhood of 1.2 nm.  
Hold on a sec, I double-checked the arithmetic by redoing the 2mK step a mite different: 2 * 9.109 * 1.602 ≈ 29.18, so 2mK ≈ 29.18e-50, sqrt of that ~5.4e-25, same as afore, so p and λ numbers stand.  
There's also that handy electron formula folks quote: λ(nm) ≈ 1.226 / sqrt(K(eV)), and for K = 1 eV that gives λ ≈ 1.226 nm, which squares with my calc, so the electron's wavelength's ~1.226–1.227 nm.

Lo, let us tackle this question. The inquirer asketh of the effects of castration upon sexual behaviour in primates compared with less-developed creatures, such as mice or birds. From the premise we know that in those lower beasts castration bringeth about a near disappearance of sexual behaviour. Now must we compare this to the effects in higher primates.

Behold the options; let us examine them one by one.

Option A saith that in higher primates, yea even men, castration doth not affect the ability to perform the sexual act if they be mature and experienced. Verily, I remember that in men castration hath been known to lessen the lust, yet perchance the bodily power to perform remaineth. But doth that prove that sexual behaviour vanish not? I wot not. Perchance there is a difference 'twixt desire and the bodily act.

Option B declareth that castration after sexual maturity lesseneth aggression but not sexual behaviour. Yet in lower beasts castration removeth sexual behaviour. If primates be more complex, perchance their behaviour is not so directly bound to hormones? But I am not certain. Methinks in some primates castration may abate aggression more than it doth sexual behaviour, yet I wouldst verify.

Option C suggesteth a temporary decline that afterward recovereth. This seemeth unlikely; for if the humours (hormones) be removed, the sexual behaviour should not recover save there be some compensatory mechanism. Yet I recall not such.

Option D affirmeth a complete loss of sexual behaviour. This contradicteth that which is known of men. Forsooth, castrated men may yet perform somewhat of sexual behaviour, albeit diminished. Thus D seemeth false.

Option E saith no effect at any stage. That is overbold. Though behaviour may not vanish utterly, there should be some effect, especially where hormones are concerned.

Option F claimeth an increase of sexual behaviour by reason of hormonal imbalance. That maketh no sense; castration removeth testosterone, which commonly lesseneth sexual behaviour, not augmenteth it.

Option G averreth that castration affecteth all animals' ability. Yet the query itself telleth that in lower creatures it doth so; therefore G is too broad and mis-setteth the matter, for the question comparèth primates with lower animals, not asserteth uniformity.

Option H pronounceth that primates cannot learn sexual behaviour by experience. That seemeth unlikely; primates lear­neth behaviours by experience, so H falleth.

Option I speaketh of a permanent shift to non-sexual social behaviour. I am uncertain; perchance some alteration in social conduct occurreth, yet not necessarily a total change.

Option J saith that castration ere puberty preventeth the development of sexual behaviour. That may be true, as when testosterone is absent in development secondary sexual marks fail to appear. Yet the question concerneth adults, not prepubertal castration.

Therefore the question toucheth adult castration in primates. The options that rise afore are A, B, D, J. Let us fix our minds upon A and B.

In lower beasts castration removeth sexual behaviour. In primates the effect may be less fierce. For example, in men, castration (as among eunuchs of old) doth lessen libido, yet they may still manifest sexual behaviour, though altered. Therefore perchance A is true. Yet B contendeth that after maturity castration lesseneth aggression but not sexual behaviour. That may be so. I hold that castration in primates doth affect sexual behaviour, though not so utterly as in lower beasts. Yet the choices afford no middle ground.

Mark well: the premise saith that in mice and birds castration causeth sexual behaviour to vanish. The query comparèth this with higher primates. Thus the correct reply must shew that in primates the effect differeth. If A sayeth that castration doth not impair the ability to perform the sexual act in those mature and practised, then this is a differing effect. Therefore A would be the answere. So I elect A.

Let us, then, set about this enquiry concerning the digestion and absorption of proteins, bearing in mind that the alternatives are lettered A through D and that our task is to discern which assertion stands in conformity with established physiological fact.

I commence with the examination of option A: “The products of protein digestion may be absorbed as free amino acids or as di- or tripeptides.” One observes that proteins are indeed subjected to proteolytic degradation into constituent amino acids and into small peptides, and that within the small intestine the action of peptidases and allied enzymes effects the division of these larger molecules into dipeptides and tripeptides; further, it is most curious that such di- and tripeptides may themselves be taken up across the intestinal epithelium and are subsequently cleaved within the enterocytes to furnish free amino acids, so that upon due consideration A appears to be in accord with the known sequence of events and thus sounds correct.

Turning to option B, which maintains that gastric digestion is equally efficient owing to the antrum’s grinding, we may note that although the stomach doth indeed churn and triturate alimentary matter, the process of proteolysis within that organ is chiefly dependent upon the enzyme pepsin and is subject to the influence of the gastric milieu, notably the hydrogen-ion concentration, and also to the intrinsic character of the protein substrate; moreover, the bulk of proteolytic activity is transacted within the small intestine rather than the stomach, so that the claim of equal efficiency is not sustained, and consequently B seems incorrect.

Concerning option C, which asserts that gastric chief cells produce chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidase A, one must correct this misapprehension by observing that the gastric chief cells are charged with the secretion of pepsinogen, the zymogen of pepsin, whereas the enzymes chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidase are the products of the pancreatic acini; therefore C is demonstrably wrong, for those enzymes do not originate from the stomachal chief cells.

Lastly, with respect to option D, which avers that merely one of the fourteen transporters is employed for absorption, we shall remark that the intestinal mucosa possesses a multiplicity of amino acid transport systems, several distinct carriers being responsible for different classes of amino acids, and that some mechanisms accommodate dipeptides and tripeptides as well; hence the proposition that only a single transporter out of fourteen is used cannot be upheld, and D is likewise incorrect.

In fine, when the several statements are weighed against the corpus of physiological knowledge, the most correct of the offered alternatives is A, while the remaining options betray inaccuracies respecting the sources of enzymes, the relative efficiency of gastric digestion, or the multiplicity of transporters concerned in absorption.
